questions.question: A running process requests a disk read whose result is required before it can execute its next instruction. The data is not available yet. In the standard Ready/Running/Blocked process-state model, which transition occurs immediately?
questions.explanation: The process must wait for the disk operation, so it moves from Running to Blocked. Ready would mean it can execute as soon as a CPU is assigned.

questions.question: Process P is blocked waiting for an I/O operation. The operation completes while another process continues running, and the scheduler does not immediately dispatch P. In the standard Ready/Running/Blocked model, which transition does P make?
questions.explanation: I/O completion removes the reason for blocking. P becomes Ready and waits for dispatch; completion of its I/O does not itself give P the CPU.

questions.question: A timer interrupt preempts process P midway through a calculation. Which information must the OS preserve as part of P's saved execution context, commonly associated with its Process Control Block (PCB), so that P can resume correctly?

options.A: P's program counter, stack pointer, and CPU register values
options.B: Only P's process identifier and scheduling priority
options.C: Only P's executable file name and total CPU time used
options.D: Only P's open-file identifiers and parent process identifier

questions.explanation: The program counter identifies the resume point, while registers and the stack pointer preserve the interrupted computation. Identifiers, priorities, accounting data, and file information alone cannot reconstruct that computation.

questions.question: A process arrives at time 3 ms, first receives the CPU at time 5 ms, and completes at time 14 ms. What is its turnaround time?
questions.explanation: Turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time: 14 - 3 = 11 ms. The first-dispatch delay, 5 - 3 = 2 ms, is the response time.

questions.question: Between arrival and completion, a process spends exactly 17 ms in the system: 6 ms executing on the CPU, 4 ms blocked for I/O, and the rest waiting in the ready queue. Scheduling overhead is zero. What is its total ready-queue waiting time?
questions.explanation: The elapsed time consists of CPU execution, I/O blocking, and ready-queue waiting. Waiting time = 17 - 6 - 4 = 7 ms; blocked time must not be counted as ready-queue waiting.

questions.question: Three processes arrive at time 0 on one CPU and enter the FCFS queue in the order P1, P2, P3. They have single CPU bursts of 6, 2, and 4 ms, respectively, with no I/O or scheduling overhead. How long does P3 wait before it starts?
questions.explanation: FCFS runs P1 from 0 to 6 and P2 from 6 to 8. P3 starts at 8, so its waiting time is 8 - 0 = 8 ms.

questions.question: P1, P2, and P3 are all ready at time 0, with single CPU bursts of 8, 3, and 5 ms, respectively. A single CPU uses non-preemptive Shortest Job First (SJF), knows the burst lengths exactly, and has zero scheduling overhead. What is the execution order?
questions.explanation: All processes are available when the CPU makes its first choice. SJF selects bursts in increasing order: 3 ms (P2), 5 ms (P3), then 8 ms (P1).

questions.question: A single CPU uses preemptive priority scheduling, with a smaller priority number indicating higher priority. P1, with priority 4, is running and still has CPU work remaining when P2, with priority 1, becomes ready. There are no other processes or scheduling overheads. What happens to P1 when P2 is dispatched?

options.A: P1 remains Running until its CPU burst ends
options.B: P1 moves from Running to Blocked
options.C: P1 moves from Running to Ready
options.D: P1 moves from Running to Terminated

questions.explanation: P2 has higher priority and preempts P1. P1 remains able to execute, so it returns to Ready; it has neither requested I/O nor finished its work.

questions.question: In steady state, a CPU repeatedly performs 3 ms of useful process execution followed by 0.3 ms of context-switch work. There is no idle time or other overhead. Approximately what percentage of elapsed time is spent on context switching?
questions.explanation: Each repeated cycle takes 3 + 0.3 = 3.3 ms. The overhead fraction is 0.3 / 3.3, or approximately 9.09%; dividing by useful execution time alone gives the wrong denominator.

questions.question: One CPU uses non-preemptive FCFS for the processes below. Each process has one CPU burst and no I/O; scheduling overhead is zero. What is the average waiting time, rounded to two decimal places? All times are in ms.
questions.code_snippet:
Process | Arrival | CPU burst
P1      | 0       | 5
P2      | 1       | 3
P3      | 2       | 1
questions.explanation: Gantt chart: P1 [0,5), P2 [5,8), P3 [8,9). Waiting times are 0, 5 - 1 = 4, and 8 - 2 = 6 ms. Their average is 10/3 = 3.33 ms.

questions.question: One CPU uses non-preemptive SJF with exact knowledge of the single CPU bursts below. There is no I/O or scheduling overhead. What is P2's turnaround time? All times are in ms.
questions.code_snippet:
Process | Arrival | CPU burst
P1      | 0       | 7
P2      | 1       | 4
P3      | 2       | 1
P4      | 3       | 2
questions.explanation: Only P1 is available at time 0, and it runs to completion. Gantt chart: P1 [0,7), P3 [7,8), P4 [8,10), P2 [10,14). P2's turnaround time is 14 - 1 = 13 ms.

questions.question: One CPU uses Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) with exact burst lengths. Each process has one CPU burst and no I/O; scheduling overhead is zero. What is the average waiting time, rounded to two decimal places? All times are in ms.
questions.code_snippet:
Process | Arrival | CPU burst
P1      | 0       | 8
P2      | 1       | 4
P3      | 2       | 2
questions.explanation: Gantt chart: P1 [0,1), P2 [1,2), P3 [2,4), P2 [4,7), P1 [7,14). Waiting time equals completion - arrival - burst: P1 = 6, P2 = 2, P3 = 0 ms. Average = 8/3 = 2.67 ms.

questions.question: P1, P2, and P3 arrive at time 0 and enter a Round Robin queue in that order. Their single CPU bursts are 5, 3, and 1 ms, respectively. The quantum is 2 ms, with no I/O or scheduling overhead. What is P2's total waiting time?
questions.explanation: Gantt chart: P1 [0,2), P2 [2,4), P3 [4,5), P1 [5,7), P2 [7,8), P1 [8,9). P2 completes at 8 ms and executes for 3 ms, giving waiting time 8 - 0 - 3 = 5 ms.

questions.question: One CPU uses Round Robin with a 3 ms quantum. P1 arrives at time 0 with a 7 ms CPU burst; P2 arrives at time 3 with a 2 ms CPU burst. There is no I/O or overhead. At a quantum boundary, new arrivals are enqueued before the expired process is requeued, and the scheduler immediately selects the queue head. What are the first three CPU allocations, treating each quantum as a separate allocation?
questions.explanation: At time 3, P2 enters the queue before P1 is requeued, so P2 runs next and finishes at 5. P1 then receives a 3 ms quantum from 5 to 8; its final 1 ms is a subsequent allocation.

questions.question: All processes below arrive at time 0 on one CPU using non-preemptive priority scheduling. Smaller priority numbers indicate higher priority. Each process has one CPU burst and no I/O; scheduling overhead is zero. What is the average turnaround time, rounded to two decimal places? Burst lengths are in ms.
questions.code_snippet:
Process | CPU burst | Priority
P1      | 4         | 3
P2      | 3         | 1
P3      | 2         | 2
questions.explanation: Gantt chart: P2 [0,3), P3 [3,5), P1 [5,9). Because all arrivals are 0, turnaround times equal completion times: 3, 5, and 9 ms. Average = 17/3 = 5.67 ms.

questions.question: One CPU uses preemptive priority scheduling, with smaller numbers indicating higher priority. Each process has one CPU burst and no I/O; scheduling overhead is zero. What is P1's total waiting time? All times are in ms.
questions.code_snippet:
Process | Arrival | CPU burst | Priority
P1      | 0       | 6         | 3
P2      | 2       | 3         | 1
P3      | 3       | 2         | 2
questions.explanation: Gantt chart: P1 [0,2), P2 [2,5), P3 [5,7), P1 [7,11). P1 waits only during [2,7), totaling 5 ms; equivalently, 11 - 0 - 6 = 5 ms.

questions.question: One CPU uses Round Robin with a 4 ms quantum and zero scheduling overhead. P1 arrives at time 0 with a single 9 ms CPU burst. P2 arrives at time 1 with a single 2 ms CPU burst and joins the ready queue. Neither process performs I/O. What are P2's response time and turnaround time, respectively?
questions.explanation: P1 runs [0,4), then P2 runs [4,6) and finishes. P2's response time is first start - arrival = 4 - 1 = 3 ms. Its turnaround time is completion - arrival = 6 - 1 = 5 ms.

questions.question: P1 and P2 arrive at time 0 and enter a non-preemptive FCFS ready queue in that order. P1 executes CPU 3 ms, blocks for I/O 4 ms, then executes CPU 2 ms. P2 executes one CPU burst of 6 ms. I/O proceeds independently of the CPU, and scheduling overhead is zero. A process returning from I/O joins the ready-queue tail. What is P1's total ready-queue waiting time?
questions.explanation: P1 runs [0,3) and performs I/O [3,7). P2 runs [3,9). P1 becomes Ready at 7, waits until 9, and runs [9,11). Its only ready-queue wait is [7,9), or 2 ms. The 4 ms of I/O is blocked time.

questions.question: An initially idle single CPU uses FCFS with zero scheduling overhead. P1 arrives at time 2 with a 3 ms CPU burst, and P2 arrives at time 8 with a 2 ms CPU burst. There are no other processes or I/O operations. Over the observation interval [0,10), what percentage of time does the CPU execute process instructions?
questions.explanation: The CPU executes P1 during [2,5) and P2 during [8,10), totaling 5 ms of useful work in a 10 ms interval. Utilization is 5/10 = 50%; the initial and intermediate idle intervals are included.

questions.question: P1, P2, and P3 arrive at time 0 and enter an FCFS queue in that order, with single CPU bursts of 4, 2, and 3 ms. Switching between two different processes costs 1 ms, during which no process instructions execute. The initial dispatch and the transition after the last completion cost nothing. There is no I/O. From time 0 until all processes finish, approximately what fraction of elapsed time is useful process execution?
questions.explanation: Useful execution totals 4 + 2 + 3 = 9 ms. Two switches add 2 ms: P1 [0,4), switch [4,5), P2 [5,7), switch [7,8), P3 [8,11). The useful fraction is 9/11 = 81.82%.

questions.question: A Round Robin system has enough continuously ready CPU-bound processes that every quantum uses its full q ms and is followed by a switch to a different process costing 1 ms. There is no idle time or other overhead. In steady state, what is the smallest integer q that keeps context-switch overhead at or below 5% of elapsed time?
questions.explanation: The overhead fraction is 1/(q + 1). Requiring 1/(q + 1) <= 0.05 gives q + 1 >= 20, or q >= 19 ms. Using q rather than q + 1 as the denominator would incorrectly require 20 ms.

questions.question: An SJF scheduler estimates future CPU bursts by exponential averaging: new_estimate = alpha * most_recent_actual_burst + (1 - alpha) * old_estimate. Initially the estimate is 8 ms and alpha = 0.25. Two actual bursts of 12 ms and then 5 ms are observed, with an update after each. What is the estimate for the next burst?
questions.explanation: After the 12 ms burst, the estimate is 0.25 * 12 + 0.75 * 8 = 9 ms. After the 5 ms burst, it becomes 0.25 * 5 + 0.75 * 9 = 8 ms. Each update must use the previous estimate.

questions.question: A single CPU uses non-preemptive priority scheduling with aging. A smaller number indicates higher priority. For a process continuously waiting in the ready queue, effective_priority = base_priority - floor(ready_wait_ms / 2). R occupies the CPU until time 6. The processes below join the ready queue at their arrival times and do not run before R finishes. With zero dispatch overhead, which process is selected at time 6, and what is its effective priority? All times are in ms.
questions.code_snippet:
Process | Arrival | Base priority
P1      | 0       | 8
P2      | 2       | 7
P3      | 4       | 5
questions.explanation: At time 6, P1 has waited 6 ms, P2 4 ms, and P3 2 ms. Their effective priorities are 8 - 3 = 5, 7 - 2 = 5, and 5 - 1 = 4. P3 has the smallest value, so it is selected.

questions.question: P is the only process in a single-CPU system and requires one 9 ms CPU burst with no I/O. Round Robin uses a 2 ms quantum and zero overhead. Count a process-to-process context switch only when the CPU changes from one process to a different process; initial dispatch, timer-handler entry/exit, and final completion do not count. How many quantum expirations occur before P finishes, and how many process-to-process context switches occur?
questions.explanation: P exhausts quanta at times 2, 4, 6, and 8 ms, then finishes at 9 before the next expiration. It is selected again each time because no other process exists. Under the stated counting rule, there are 4 expirations and 0 process-to-process switches.

questions.question: One CPU uses SRTF for the single-burst processes below, with no I/O. A preemption or completion followed by another process requires a 1 ms dispatch interval with no useful execution. Initial dispatch at time 0 is free. Dispatch intervals cannot be interrupted or restarted; all arrivals through the end of an interval are considered when choosing the shortest remaining process at that end, with no extra dispatch cost for changing the tentative choice. No dispatch is charged after the final completion. Waiting time includes all time after arrival when a process is unfinished but not executing. What is the average waiting time, rounded to two decimal places? All times are in ms.
questions.code_snippet:
Process | Arrival | CPU burst
P1      | 0       | 7
P2      | 2       | 3
P3      | 3       | 1
questions.explanation: P1 runs [0,2), leaving 5 ms. During dispatch [2,3), P3 arrives and is chosen at 3. The rest is P3 [3,4), dispatch [4,5), P2 [5,8), dispatch [8,9), P1 [9,14). Waiting times are 14 - 0 - 7 = 7, 8 - 2 - 3 = 3, and 4 - 3 - 1 = 0 ms. Average = 10/3 = 3.33 ms.

questions.question: P1, P2, and P3 arrive at time 0 in that Round Robin queue order, with single CPU bursts of 5, 4, and 2 ms. The quantum is 2 ms. Every change from one process to a different process, including after a completion, costs 1 ms with no useful execution. Initial dispatch and the transition after the final completion are free. There is no I/O. What is the average turnaround time, rounded to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: Useful execution intervals are P1 [0,2), P2 [3,5), P3 [6,8), P1 [9,11), P2 [12,14), P1 [15,16), with 1 ms switches between them. Completion times are P1 = 16, P2 = 14, and P3 = 8. Since all arrive at 0, average turnaround = (16 + 14 + 8)/3 = 12.67 ms.

questions.question: One CPU uses preemptive priority scheduling with smaller numbers indicating higher priority and zero scheduling overhead. I/O proceeds independently of the CPU. P1 and P2 are ready at time 0. P1 has priority 1 and performs CPU 2 ms, I/O 4 ms, then CPU 2 ms. P2 has priority 2 and needs CPU 7 ms with no I/O. P3 arrives at time 3 with priority 0 and needs CPU 2 ms with no I/O. Returning from I/O immediately makes a process eligible to preempt. What is P2's total ready-queue waiting time?
questions.explanation: P1 runs [0,2) and performs I/O [2,6). P2 runs [2,3), P3 [3,5), and P2 [5,6). P1 returns and preempts P2, running [6,8). P2 finishes in [8,13). P2 waits during [0,2), [3,5), and [6,8): 6 ms total, also 13 - 0 - 7.

questions.question: One CPU uses SRTF for the single-burst processes below, with no I/O or scheduling overhead. An arrival preempts the running process only if its burst is strictly less than the running process's remaining time; on equality the running process continues. When selecting from the ready queue, ties use earlier original arrival time, then smaller process number. What is the average waiting time? All times are in ms.
questions.code_snippet:
Process | Arrival | CPU burst
P1      | 0       | 6
P2      | 1       | 4
P3      | 2       | 3
P4      | 4       | 1
questions.explanation: P1 runs [0,1), then P2 [1,5). P3's burst equals P2's remaining 3 ms at time 2, and P4's burst equals P2's remaining 1 ms at time 4, so neither preempts. Then P4 runs [5,6), P3 [6,9), P1 [9,14). Waiting times are 8, 0, 4, and 1 ms. Average = 13/4 = 3.25 ms.

questions.question: One CPU uses Round Robin with a 2 ms quantum and zero overhead. P1 and P2 arrive at time 0 in that queue order. P1 performs CPU 3 ms, I/O 3 ms, then CPU 1 ms. P2 needs one CPU burst of 5 ms. P3 arrives at time 3 and needs one CPU burst of 2 ms. I/O proceeds independently of the CPU. Arrivals and I/O completions join the ready-queue tail immediately and do not preempt the running quantum; at a quantum boundary, these events are enqueued before the expired process is requeued. A process blocks as soon as its current CPU burst finishes, even if that occurs before quantum expiration. What is P1's total ready-queue waiting time?
questions.explanation: Gantt chart: P1 [0,2), P2 [2,4), P1 [4,5), P3 [5,7), P2 [7,9), P1 [9,10), P2 [10,11). P1 performs I/O [5,8), so it joins the queue during P2's quantum and runs before P2's final 1 ms. P1 waits during [2,4) and [8,9), totaling 3 ms; equivalently, 10 - 0 - 4 CPU - 3 I/O = 3 ms.

questions.question: The workload below is run separately on one CPU under FCFS, non-preemptive SJF, and SRTF. Each process has one CPU burst and no I/O; all three schedulers have exact burst knowledge and zero scheduling overhead. They never leave the CPU idle when a process is ready. Which tuple gives the average waiting times in the order (FCFS, SJF, SRTF)? All times are in ms.
questions.code_snippet:
Process | Arrival | CPU burst
P1      | 0       | 7
P2      | 2       | 4
P3      | 4       | 1
questions.explanation: FCFS runs P1 [0,7), P2 [7,11), P3 [11,12): waits 0, 5, 7, averaging 4 ms. SJF runs P1 [0,7), P3 [7,8), P2 [8,12): waits 0, 6, 3, averaging 3 ms. SRTF runs P1 [0,2), P2 [2,4), P3 [4,5), P2 [5,7), P1 [7,12): waits 5, 1, 0, averaging 2 ms.

questions.question: Two threads each increment a shared counter once using a separate atomic read and atomic write, without a lock. Memory is sequentially consistent. The counter initially equals 10, and the exact interleaving below occurs. What is its final value?
questions.code_snippet:
T1: local1 = counter   // reads 10
T2: local2 = counter   // reads 10
T1: counter = local1 + 1
T2: counter = local2 + 1
questions.explanation: Both local variables contain 10, so both writes store 11. One increment is lost because the read-modify-write sequence is not atomic, even though each individual read and write is atomic.

questions.question: An execution log shows T1 entering a critical section, T2 entering the same critical section before T1 exits, and then both threads exiting. Which critical-section requirement does this observed execution directly violate?

options.A: Mutual exclusion: at most one thread may be inside that critical section
options.B: Progress: a choice among interested threads must not be postponed indefinitely
options.C: Bounded waiting: a waiting thread may be overtaken only a bounded number of times
options.D: FIFO admission: threads must enter in the order in which they request entry

questions.explanation: The overlapping entries directly demonstrate a failure of mutual exclusion. The log does not demonstrate indefinite postponement or unbounded overtaking. FIFO admission is a separate policy and is not required by every correct critical-section solution.

questions.question: Two threads use strict alternation as shown. The shared atomic variable turn initially equals 0, and memory is sequentially consistent. T0 stays in its remainder section forever without requesting entry. T1 wants to enter and keeps taking execution steps. The critical section is empty, but T1 spins forever. Which requirement is directly violated because a thread that does not want entry prevents admission?
questions.code_snippet:
Thread Ti, where j = 1 - i:
while true:
    while turn != i: pass
    critical_section()
    turn = j
    remainder_section()

options.A: Mutual exclusion, because both threads enter simultaneously
options.B: Atomicity of reads, because T1 must observe a torn turn value
options.C: Lock ownership, because T1 releases T0's mutex
options.D: Progress, because the empty critical section remains unavailable to the interested thread

questions.explanation: Strict alternation makes T1 depend on T0 changing turn even though T0 does not want to enter. A thread in its remainder section must not prevent an interested thread from entering an otherwise empty critical section. This is a progress violation.

questions.question: A lock provides mutual exclusion and allows some interested thread to enter whenever the critical section becomes free. However, for every integer N, there is a legal execution in which at least N other critical-section entries occur after thread T requests the lock and before T is admitted. Which additional standard critical-section guarantee is missing?

options.B: Progress in choosing some interested thread for an empty critical section
options.D: Ownership enforcement when a thread releases the lock

questions.explanation: Bounded waiting requires a finite bound on how many times other threads may enter after T requests admission. The stated family of executions has no such bound, even if T eventually enters in each individual execution.

questions.question: A design needs thread A to notify thread B that an event has occurred. A may notify before B starts waiting. The mutex API permits only the owning thread to unlock, while the counting-semaphore API has no ownership restriction. Which implementation supports this one-event handoff?

options.A: B locks a mutex, and A unlocks that mutex to notify B
options.B: Initialize semaphore S to 0; A calls signal(S), and B calls wait(S)
options.C: Initialize semaphore S to 1; A calls signal(S), and B calls wait(S)
options.D: Initialize semaphore S to 0; A and B both call wait(S)

questions.explanation: A signal on a zero-initialized counting semaphore either wakes B or leaves a permit for B's later wait. Initializing it to 1 lets B pass before the event. Cross-thread mutex unlocking violates the stated ownership rule, and two waits provide no notification.

questions.question: A counting semaphore S starts with 3 available permits. Two threads each successfully execute wait(S) once, and neither has executed signal(S). No other operations occur. How many permits remain available?
questions.explanation: Each successful wait consumes one permit. The remaining available count is 3 - 2 = 1, so neither of the two waits blocks.

questions.question: A bounded buffer has capacity 8 and already contains 3 items when its synchronization objects are initialized. No producer or consumer operation is in progress. The standard design uses counting semaphores empty and full for available slots and items, plus binary semaphore mutex for exclusive buffer access. What initial values should (empty, full, mutex) have?
questions.explanation: Five slots are free and three items are available, so empty = 8 - 3 = 5 and full = 3. The initially unlocked binary semaphore mutex has one permit.

questions.question: A resource-allocation policy requires a process to release every resource it holds before waiting for any additional resource. Which Coffman condition does this policy directly eliminate?

options.B: Circular wait by imposing an explicit global resource order
options.D: No preemption by forcibly taking resources from their owners

questions.explanation: A process may no longer hold resources while waiting to acquire others. The policy does not make resources shareable, impose a global ordering, or forcibly preempt an owner's resources. Removing hold and wait prevents the four necessary deadlock conditions from holding together.

questions.question: Non-recursive mutexes A and B each have one instance. T1 holds A and blocks acquiring B. T2 holds B and blocks acquiring A. Neither thread releases its held mutex before the requested acquisition succeeds; there are no timeouts, cancellations, or forced releases. What is the resulting state?

options.A: Only temporary contention; either blocked thread can independently finish
options.B: Deadlock, with both threads waiting in a cycle
options.C: A lost update, but both threads can keep executing their critical sections
options.D: Livelock, with both threads repeatedly releasing and reacquiring their mutexes

questions.explanation: Each thread waits for a mutex held by the other, and neither can reach its release operation. Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait all hold, producing deadlock.

questions.question: A shared integer x initially equals 5. T1 increments it once and T2 decrements it once using the pseudocode below. Each read and write is atomic, but each read-modify-write pair is not. Memory is sequentially consistent, each thread preserves its own program order, and both threads finish. What is the complete set of possible final values of x?
questions.code_snippet:
T1:                         T2:
    a = read(x)                 b = read(x)
    write(x, a + 1)             write(x, b - 1)
questions.explanation: If one thread completes before the other's read, the updates combine and x ends at 5. If both read 5 first, their writes store 6 and 4, so the last write determines a final value of 6 or 4. These cases exhaust all program-order-preserving interleavings.

questions.question: Two threads each execute the loop below exactly 1,000 times and both finish. The shared integer x initially equals 0 and does not overflow. Both use the same initially unlocked mutex m. All accesses to x are inside the shown critical section, and lock/unlock provide normal mutual exclusion and visibility guarantees. What is x after both threads finish?
questions.code_snippet:
repeat 1000 times:
    lock(m)
    local = x
    x = local + 1
    unlock(m)
questions.explanation: The mutex serializes each entire read-modify-write sequence, so none of the 2,000 increments is lost. Each thread completes 1,000 increments, giving x = 2,000 regardless of the order of critical-section entries.

questions.question: Use this signed-counter semaphore model: atomic wait(S) decrements S and blocks the caller if the result is negative; atomic signal(S) increments S and, if the result is at most 0, wakes one FIFO waiter. A woken wait is already satisfied and does not decrement again. S starts at 1. Execute the operations below in order; a blocked caller takes no further steps until woken. What are the final signed counter and the set of threads still blocked on S?
questions.code_snippet:
A: wait(S)
B: wait(S)
C: wait(S)
A: signal(S)
D: wait(S)
B: signal(S)
questions.explanation: The counter follows 1 -> 0 -> -1 -> -2 -> -1 -> -2 -> -1. A's signal wakes B, leaving C queued. D then queues behind C. B's signal wakes C, leaving only D blocked. A resumed wait consumes no second permit.

questions.question: Use a nonnegative counting-semaphore model: wait consumes an available permit or blocks if there is none. signal hands a permit directly to the oldest waiter, keeping the available count at 0, or increments the available count if no waiter exists. S starts at 0 and has no ownership restriction. The operations below execute in order, with no extra waits or signals by woken threads. What is the final available count, and which threads remain blocked?
questions.code_snippet:
A: wait(S)
B: wait(S)
C: signal(S)
D: signal(S)
E: signal(S)
questions.explanation: A and B initially block. C's signal satisfies A's wait, and D's signal satisfies B's wait, without accumulating available permits. E's signal finds no waiters and leaves one available permit.

questions.question: A bounded buffer is full. There is exactly one producer and one consumer, and no operation is initially in progress. The producer executes first and reaches its second wait in the code below. All waits are blocking, mutex is initially 1, empty is 0, and full equals the buffer capacity. There are no cancellations or other threads. What happens when the consumer then runs?
questions.code_snippet:
Producer:                 Consumer:
    wait(mutex)               wait(full)
    wait(empty)               wait(mutex)
    insert_item()             remove_item()
    signal(mutex)             signal(mutex)
    signal(full)              signal(empty)

options.A: The consumer removes an item, allowing the producer to continue
options.B: The producer overwrites an existing item without waiting
options.C: Both block: the producer needs an empty slot, while the consumer needs the producer's mutex
options.D: The consumer blocks on full before it can attempt mutex

questions.explanation: The producer acquires mutex and blocks on empty while still holding mutex. The consumer can pass wait(full), but then blocks on mutex and cannot remove an item or signal empty. The producer must wait for empty before acquiring mutex in the standard solution.

questions.question: A capacity-5 buffer starts empty with (empty, full, mutex) = (5, 0, 1). A correct producer waits on empty and mutex, inserts one item, then signals mutex and full. A correct consumer waits on full and mutex, removes one item, then signals mutex and empty. Three complete productions occur, then one complete consumption, then two complete productions. There are no in-progress operations at the end. What is the final tuple (empty, full, mutex)?
questions.explanation: The final occupancy is 0 + 3 - 1 + 2 = 4 items. Because every operation has completed, full = 4 and empty = 5 - 4 = 1. Each critical section releases mutex, restoring it to 1.

questions.question: A shared atomic integer x starts at 0, and counting semaphore ready starts at 0. Memory and semaphore operations are sequentially consistent, and each thread preserves its program order. Both threads finish. What is the complete set of values that T2 can print?
questions.code_snippet:
T1:                      T2:
    signal(ready)             wait(ready)
    x = 42                    print(x)

options.D: No value; T2 necessarily remains blocked

questions.explanation: T2's wait cannot finish before T1 signals, but the signal precedes the write to x. T2 can therefore print before the write and see 0, or after it and see 42. Moving the write before signal would establish the required publication order.

questions.question: The correct reader-preference protocol below uses initially available binary semaphores count_mutex and resource. Two readers R1 and R2 have completed entry and are reading, so reader_count is 2. R1 completes its entire exit, then writer W calls wait(resource) and blocks, then R2 completes its entire exit. A signal to a waiting thread directly transfers the permit; the available semaphore count stays 0. Immediately after R2's exit, W's wait has returned, but W has not released resource. What is (reader_count, available resource permits, available count_mutex permits)?
questions.code_snippet:
Reader entry:
    wait(count_mutex)
    reader_count += 1
    if reader_count == 1: wait(resource)
    signal(count_mutex)
Reader exit:
    wait(count_mutex)
    reader_count -= 1
    if reader_count == 0: signal(resource)
    signal(count_mutex)
Writer: wait(resource); write_data(); signal(resource)
questions.explanation: R1's exit reduces reader_count from 2 to 1 without releasing resource. R2 reduces it to 0 and signals resource, transferring the permit to W. W holds that permit, so its available count is 0. R2 releases count_mutex, leaving it at 1.

questions.question: A reader-preference readers-writers implementation allows a new reader to join whenever another reader is active, even if a writer is waiting. Every reader eventually exits, but an unending sequence of overlapping readers keeps the active-reader count above zero. The waiting writer keeps getting scheduled but cannot acquire the protected resource. Which problem does this execution demonstrate?

options.A: A deadlock cycle that also prevents all readers from finishing
options.B: A violation of mutual exclusion between the writer and an active reader
options.C: A lost update to reader_count, even when that count is correctly locked
options.D: Writer starvation despite continuing reader progress

questions.explanation: Readers continue to enter and finish, but the reader count never reaches the value needed to release the resource to the writer. This is writer starvation; neither deadlock nor a reader_count race is needed for it to occur.

questions.question: A correct writer-preference readers-writers policy prevents new readers from entering while any writer is waiting; existing readers may finish. R1 is reading when W1 requests exclusive access. R2 then requests read access before R1 exits. There are no other arrivals, and each admitted operation finishes. What is the admission order after R1 exits?

options.A: R2 enters and finishes before W1
options.C: W1 enters and finishes before R2
options.D: Neither W1 nor R2 can ever enter

questions.explanation: W1's pending request closes admission to new readers, so R2 must wait even while R1 is still reading. When R1 exits, W1 gains exclusive access. Once W1 finishes and no writer remains pending, R2 may enter.

questions.question: T1 needs mutexes A then B, while T2 needs B then A. Instead of blocking on the second mutex, each performs try_lock, releases its first mutex on failure, and retries. A legal schedule repeats these steps forever: T1 locks A; T2 locks B; both try_lock calls fail before either first mutex is released; both release; both retry. Neither thread blocks inside try_lock, and neither reaches its useful critical section. What does this execution demonstrate?

options.A: Livelock: the threads keep acting but make no useful progress
options.B: Deadlock: both threads remain blocked forever while holding their mutexes
options.C: A mutual-exclusion violation: both threads hold A simultaneously
options.D: Only T1 starves while T2 repeatedly completes its useful critical section

questions.explanation: The release-and-retry policy avoids the shown blocking deadlock, but this schedule makes both threads repeatedly undo their partial acquisitions. They continue executing without entering their useful critical sections, which is livelock.

questions.question: For the Banker’s Algorithm snapshot below, vectors list resource types (A, B). Need = Max - Allocation, and a process that can obtain its remaining Need may finish and release its entire allocation. Available is (1, 1). Which listed order is a safe sequence?
questions.explanation: Need vectors are P0 = (1,1), P1 = (1,1), P2 = (2,0). Starting Work = (1,1), P1 can finish, producing Work = (1,2). P0 then finishes, producing (2,2), which satisfies P2. P2 cannot start initially or immediately after P1.

questions.question: In the Banker’s Algorithm snapshot below, Available = (1, 1), and resource vectors use (A, B). P2 requests (1, 0) additional units. Apply both the initial request checks and the tentative-allocation safety test. What should the banker do?
questions.code_snippet:
Process | Allocation | Max
P0      | (1, 0)     | (2, 1)
P1      | (0, 1)     | (1, 2)
P2      | (1, 1)     | (3, 1)
Request by P2: (1, 0)

options.A: Grant it, because the request fits both P2's Need and Available
options.B: Reject it as exceeding P2's declared remaining Need
options.C: Defer it because one requested resource is currently unavailable
options.D: Defer it because the tentative allocation is unsafe

questions.explanation: P2's original Need is (2,0), so the request passes both initial checks. A tentative grant leaves Available = (0,1), with Needs (1,1), (1,1), and (1,0). Every process still needs at least one A unit, so none can finish first in the safety test. The grant must be rolled back and deferred.

questions.question: A Banker’s Algorithm safety test finds no safe sequence for a valid resource-allocation snapshot. The Max entries are upper bounds: actual future requests may be smaller, and a process may finish without using its full declared maximum. No current request or blocking information is supplied. Which conclusion is justified?

options.A: Every unfinished process is already blocked in a deadlock
options.B: The snapshot is unsafe: completion cannot be guaranteed against the declared maximum demands, but current deadlock is not established
options.C: Every possible future execution must deadlock, even if processes request less than their maxima
options.D: The snapshot is safe as long as at least one process is currently executing instructions

questions.explanation: Unsafe means no completion sequence can be guaranteed using the declared remaining maximum demands. It does not prove an existing deadlock, because actual outstanding requests are unknown and processes might finish with smaller demands. Executing instructions also does not by itself prove safety.

questions.question: Resource type A has two interchangeable instances, and B has one. P1 holds one A and waits for B. P2 holds B and waits for one A. P3 holds the other A and needs no additional resources; it will finish and release A. A process releases all held resources when it finishes, and there are no future requests beyond those stated. Although the resource-allocation graph contains a cycle through P1 and P2, which conclusion is correct?

options.A: All three processes are deadlocked because any resource-allocation cycle is sufficient
options.B: There is no deadlock: P3 can finish, then P2, then P1
options.C: P1 and P2 remain deadlocked even after P3 releases its A instance
options.D: P3 can finish, but P1 and P2 require an abort or an extra resource instance to finish

questions.explanation: P3's release supplies the A instance P2 needs. P2 can then finish and release B, allowing P1 to finish. With multiple instances of a resource type, a cycle in the resource-allocation graph alone does not prove deadlock.

questions.question: The Banker’s Algorithm snapshot below has Available = (3, 3, 2), with vectors ordered (A, B, C). P1 requests (1, 0, 2). If the request is tentatively granted, which listed sequence certifies that the resulting state is safe? Each process releases its allocation when it finishes.
questions.explanation: The request fits P1's Need (1,2,2) and Available. After granting it, Work = (2,3,0), P1's Allocation = (3,0,2), and its Need = (0,2,0). Finishing P1, P3, P4, P0, and P2 changes Work successively to (5,3,2), (7,4,3), (7,4,5), (7,5,5), and (10,5,7). Each next Need fits the current Work. None of P0, P2, or P4 can be first after the grant.

questions.question: For the Banker’s Algorithm snapshot below, Available = (0, 1) in resource order (A, B). An administrator may add x new A instances to the available pool, where x is a nonnegative integer; no B instances, allocations, or Max claims change. What is the smallest x that makes the snapshot safe?
questions.explanation: Needs are (2,1), (1,1), (2,0), and (2,1). With x = 0 no process can finish first. With x = 1 only P1 can finish, but it releases no A, leaving Work = (1,2), which still cannot satisfy any remaining process. With x = 2, the sequence P1, P0, P2, P3 is safe. Thus the minimum is 2, not merely the 1 needed to enable an initial completion.

questions.question: In the Banker’s Algorithm snapshot below, Available = (1, 1) and resource vectors use (A, B). Count distinct permutations of all four process identifiers that satisfy the safety test, with each process finishing and releasing its allocation before the next process in the permutation is considered. How many safe sequences exist?
questions.explanation: Needs are (1,1), (1,1), (2,0), and (3,1). The safe permutations are P0-P1-P2-P3, P0-P2-P1-P3, P0-P2-P3-P1, and P1-P0-P2-P3. Only P0 or P1 can start. After P1 starts, P0 must be next; after P0 starts, P2 must finish before P3 can become eligible. These constraints leave exactly four permutations.

questions.question: Consider the flawed reader entry below. count_mutex protects reader_count, which starts at 0, and resource excludes a writer from readers. Writer W already holds resource and is writing. R1 increments reader_count to 1, records first = true, releases count_mutex, and blocks at wait(resource). Before W releases resource, R2 executes its entire entry. Memory is sequentially consistent. What happens?
questions.code_snippet:
Reader entry (first is thread-local):
    wait(count_mutex)
    reader_count += 1
    first = (reader_count == 1)
    signal(count_mutex)
    if first:
        wait(resource)
    read_shared_data()

Writer: wait(resource); write_shared_data(); signal(resource)

options.A: R2 starts reading while W writes, violating reader-writer exclusion
options.B: R2 blocks on resource because every reader executes wait(resource)
options.C: R2 blocks on count_mutex because R1 holds it while waiting for resource
options.D: R2 safely reads because a positive reader_count proves a reader already owns resource

questions.explanation: R2 increments reader_count from 1 to 2, records first = false, and skips wait(resource). R1 has not acquired resource, so W is still writing when R2 reads. Protecting reader_count alone is insufficient: in the standard first-reader protocol, the first reader keeps count_mutex until it has acquired resource, preventing another reader from bypassing that pending acquisition.

questions.question: A correct capacity-5 bounded buffer initially contains 2 items, with available semaphore counts empty = 3, full = 2, mutex = 1. Each producer executes wait(empty), wait(mutex), insert, signal(mutex), signal(full). Each consumer executes wait(full), wait(mutex), remove, signal(mutex), signal(empty). The exact successful operations below occur; all threads then pause with no other operations. P1 has not yet signaled full, C1 has not yet signaled empty, and P2 has not inserted. What is the tuple (available empty permits, available full permits, physical items in the buffer)?
questions.code_snippet:
P1: wait(empty)
P2: wait(empty)
C1: wait(full)
P1: wait(mutex); insert one item; signal(mutex)
C1: wait(mutex); remove one item; signal(mutex)
questions.explanation: The two producer reservations reduce empty from 3 to 1. C1's reservation reduces full from 2 to 1. Inserting and then removing changes physical occupancy from 2 to 3 and back to 2. Neither pending signal has occurred. During in-progress operations, full need not equal physical occupancy, and empty + full need not equal capacity because permits can be reserved or awaiting publication.

questions.question: Four processes each hold one distinct single-instance resource R0 through R3, with Pi holding Ri. They are blocked waiting for the additional resource sets below; each process needs its entire requested set before it can finish. No new requests will be made, and finishing releases all held resources. Recovery may abort selected processes, canceling their requests and immediately releasing their holdings. Which listed abort set has minimum possible size and allows every surviving process to finish?
questions.explanation: The wait-for graph contains cycles P0-P1-P0, P1-P2-P1, and P2-P3-P2. The disjoint first and third cycles require at least two victims. Aborting P0 and P2 frees R0 and R2, allowing P1 to finish and leaving R2 available for P3 as well. The other listed pairs leave, respectively, the P2-P3, P0-P1, or P1-P2 cycle intact. Thus the selected two-process set is sufficient and minimum-sized.

questions.question: A byte-addressable system uses fixed-size pages of 4 KiB, where 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes. How many bits of a virtual address form the page offset?
questions.explanation: A 4 KiB page contains 4,096 = 2^12 individually addressable bytes, so the low 12 address bits select a byte within the page.

questions.question: A byte-addressable virtual memory uses 4,096-byte pages, numbered from 0. For decimal virtual address 13,500, what is the pair (virtual page number, byte offset)?
questions.explanation: 13,500 = 3 * 4,096 + 1,212. The quotient gives virtual page 3, and the remainder gives byte offset 1,212.

questions.question: A byte-addressable system uses 1,024-byte pages and equally sized physical frames, both numbered from 0. Virtual page 2 is resident in physical frame 7, and the access is permitted. What decimal physical address corresponds to decimal virtual address 2,148?
questions.explanation: The virtual address is 2 * 1,024 + 100, so its offset is 100. Paging preserves that offset: physical address = 7 * 1,024 + 100 = 7,268.

questions.question: A process has one contiguous 10 KiB region that begins on a page boundary. All of it is allocated using whole 4 KiB pages, and its final page cannot be shared with another allocation. Ignoring page-table storage, how much internal fragmentation does this allocation have? Here 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes.
questions.explanation: The region needs ceil(10/4) = 3 pages, reserving 12 KiB. The unused 12 - 10 = 2 KiB within the last allocated page is internal fragmentation.

questions.question: In a byte-addressable segmentation system, segment S has physical base 8,000 and length 1,200 bytes. Legal offsets satisfy 0 <= offset < length, and the requested access is permitted. What is the decimal physical address of (S, offset 1,199)?
questions.explanation: Offset 1,199 is less than the 1,200-byte length, so it is valid. Segmentation adds the offset to the base: 8,000 + 1,199 = 9,199.

questions.question: A byte-addressable segment has physical base 8,000 and length 1,200 bytes, with legal offsets 0 through 1,199. There is no paging. What happens when a process attempts to read one byte at offset 1,200 in this segment?

options.A: The byte is read from physical address 9,200
options.B: The offset wraps to 0, and the byte is read from physical address 8,000
options.C: A segment-bounds exception occurs before the data read
options.D: A missing-page exception loads another page and makes this offset valid

questions.explanation: A segment length is a byte count, not an inclusive largest offset. Offset 1,200 equals the length and is out of bounds. The system has no paging, and loading a page would not repair an invalid segment offset.

questions.question: A permitted read misses in the TLB. A hardware page-table walk finds a valid, present mapping for the virtual page, and the referenced data is already in physical memory. No other exception occurs. Which action is required to complete the access?

options.A: Use the resident mapping found by the walk and access the data without a page-in from storage
options.B: Load the page from storage because every TLB miss is a page fault
options.C: Terminate the process because every TLB miss indicates an invalid virtual address
options.D: Choose a page-replacement victim before the resident mapping can be used

questions.explanation: A TLB caches translations, so its miss only means the translation is not cached. A present, permitted page-table mapping can resolve the miss without storage I/O or page replacement.

questions.question: A process accesses a valid, readable virtual page that is backed by storage but is not currently resident. This demand-paging system has an available free frame, and the page-in succeeds. Which sequence describes how the access completes?

options.A: Read the requested data directly from the non-present physical frame without a fault
options.B: Report a permanent address error because a nonresident page can never be valid
options.C: Change only the TLB entry and retry without loading the missing page
options.D: Raise a page fault, load the page, update its mapping, and retry the access

questions.explanation: Nonresidency triggers a page fault, but the virtual address and permission are valid. The OS can use the free frame, load the page, install a present mapping, and restart the faulting access. No victim is needed when a free frame is available.

questions.question: After more processes are admitted, the system spends most of its time paging, CPU utilization falls, and the active processes' combined working sets exceed available frames. Which immediate policy change most directly addresses this thrashing condition?

options.A: Admit more processes whenever CPU utilization falls
options.B: Suspend some active processes and reassign their frames to the remaining working sets
options.C: Reduce every active process's frame allocation to make room for more processes
options.D: Switch to shorter CPU time slices while leaving all frame allocations unchanged

questions.explanation: Reducing the degree of multiprogramming releases frames so the remaining processes can keep their working sets resident. Adding processes or shrinking already inadequate resident sets increases memory pressure; changing CPU time slices does not resolve the frame shortage.

questions.question: A byte-addressable system has a 32-bit virtual address space and 4 KiB pages. A process uses a flat page table with one 8-byte entry for every virtual page, including unmapped pages. Ignoring other metadata, what is the page table's size? Here 1 KiB = 2^10 bytes and 1 MiB = 2^20 bytes.
questions.explanation: The 12-bit offset leaves 32 - 12 = 20 virtual-page-number bits. The flat table therefore has 2^20 entries, each 8 bytes, for 2^23 bytes = 8 MiB. The process's actual resident-page count does not shrink this stipulated flat table.

questions.question: A byte-addressable system uses 32-bit virtual addresses, 4 KiB pages, and a two-level page table. Every second-level table occupies one 4 KiB page, contains 4-byte entries, and is indexed using all of its entries. What is the virtual-address split (first-level index bits, second-level index bits, offset bits)? Here 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes.
questions.explanation: The page offset uses 12 bits. A second-level table has 4,096/4 = 1,024 = 2^10 entries, requiring a 10-bit second-level index. The remaining 32 - 12 - 10 = 10 bits form the first-level index.

questions.question: A 32-bit virtual address is split into 10 first-level index bits, 10 second-level index bits, and 12 offset bits. The root and each second-level table occupy 4 KiB. The root always exists; a second-level table exists only if it contains at least one mapped page. Exactly the four page-aligned virtual addresses below are mapped, with no other mappings or shared page-table pages. Excluding data frames, how much page-table memory is allocated? Here 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes.
questions.code_snippet:
Mapped virtual page starts:
0x00000000
0x00001000
0x00400000
0x00C00000
questions.explanation: One second-level table covers 2^(10 + 12) = 4 MiB. The addresses have first-level indices 0, 0, 1, and 3, requiring three second-level tables. Including the root, four 4 KiB table pages occupy 16 KiB.

questions.question: A byte-addressable machine supports 40-bit physical addresses and 8 KiB pages. Each page-table entry must store the entire physical frame number plus six independent flag bits, with no other fields. Hardware permits entry sizes of 4, 8, 16, or 32 bytes. What is the smallest supported entry size that can represent every frame and all flags? Here 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes.
questions.explanation: An 8 KiB page uses 13 offset bits, so the physical frame number needs 40 - 13 = 27 bits. Adding six flags requires 33 bits. Four bytes hold only 32 bits; the smallest permitted size that fits is 8 bytes.

questions.question: A system has a single-level page table and serial TLB lookup. The TLB lookup takes 10 ns and hits on 80% of references. Each physical-memory access takes 100 ns. A hit needs one data-memory access after lookup; a miss needs one page-table-memory access and then one data-memory access, with no second TLB lookup. There are no caches, page faults, or other costs. What is the effective access time?
questions.explanation: A hit costs 10 + 100 = 110 ns, and a miss costs 10 + 100 + 100 = 210 ns. The weighted mean is 0.8 * 110 + 0.2 * 210 = 130 ns. TLB lookup time is charged on both paths.

questions.question: A byte-addressable system has a two-level page table and a serial TLB lookup costing 5 ns, with a 95% hit rate. Each physical-memory access costs 80 ns. A hit needs only the data access after lookup; a miss walks both page-table levels and then accesses the data, without another TLB lookup. There are no page-walk caches, data caches, page faults, or overlapping operations. What is the mean access time?
questions.explanation: The hit path costs 5 + 80 = 85 ns. The miss path costs 5 + 3 * 80 = 245 ns because it includes two page-table reads and one data read. Mean = 0.95 * 85 + 0.05 * 245 = 93 ns.

questions.question: A single-level paging system has serial TLB lookup time 10 ns and physical-memory access time 100 ns. A hit takes one data-memory access after lookup; a miss takes one page-table-memory access followed by one data-memory access, with no extra lookup. There are no page faults or caches. What is the minimum TLB hit rate needed for a mean access time of at most 120 ns?
questions.explanation: Let h be the hit rate. Mean time = 110h + 210(1 - h) = 210 - 100h ns. Requiring 210 - 100h <= 120 gives h >= 0.90, so the minimum is 90%.

questions.question: For each logical memory reference, the probability of a page fault is 0.00001. A reference without a page fault takes 100 ns in total. A reference with a fault takes 8 ms in total, measured from the initial attempt through successful completion of the restarted access; this already includes all lookup and retry costs. What is the mean reference time, rounded to the nearest nanosecond? Use 1 ms = 1,000,000 ns.
questions.explanation: Mean = (1 - 0.00001) * 100 + 0.00001 * 8,000,000 = 179.999 ns, which rounds to 180 ns. The 8 ms fault path is already a total, so another normal-access charge must not be added to it.

questions.question: A logical memory reference faults with probability 0.0002; otherwise it takes 200 ns. Every fault evicts one page. Conditional on a fault, the victim is clean with probability 0.7 and dirty with probability 0.3. The total faulting-reference time, including all I/O and the successful retry, is 5 ms for a clean victim and 13 ms for a dirty victim. What is the mean reference time, rounded to two decimal places in microseconds? Use 1 ms = 1,000 microseconds and 1 microsecond = 1,000 ns.
questions.explanation: The conditional mean fault time is 0.7 * 5 + 0.3 * 13 = 7.4 ms = 7,400,000 ns. Overall mean = 0.9998 * 200 + 0.0002 * 7,400,000 = 1,679.96 ns = 1.67996 microseconds, rounding to 1.68.

questions.question: A byte-addressable segmented-paging system uses 2,048-byte pages and equally sized physical frames. Segment S is 6,000 bytes long; a one-byte reference is legal only if its segment-relative byte position is less than 6,000. The segment's page table is shown below, and all listed mappings are present and readable. What decimal physical address corresponds to (segment S, page 2, offset 100)? Page and frame numbers start at 0.
questions.code_snippet:
Page within S | Physical frame
0             | 4
1             | 1
2             | 9

options.D: Bounds exception because S is not an exact multiple of the page size

questions.explanation: The segment-relative position is 2 * 2,048 + 100 = 4,196, which is below 6,000. Page 2 maps to frame 9, so the physical address is 9 * 2,048 + 100 = 18,532. A partially used last page does not invalidate offsets inside the segment length.

questions.question: A process has three initially empty page frames and uses FIFO replacement. The page-reference string below contains only valid reads. Count every first load as a page fault; a hit does not change FIFO order. How many page faults occur?
questions.code_snippet: Reference string: 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5
questions.explanation: The first references to 1, 2, and 3 fault. The next 1 hits without refreshing its FIFO position. Loading 4 evicts 1; the following 2 still hits. Loading 5 evicts 2. The fault/hit pattern is F, F, F, H, F, H, F, totaling 5 faults.

questions.question: A process has three initially empty page frames and uses exact LRU replacement. Every successful reference, including a hit, refreshes the page's recency. All references below are valid reads, and every first load counts as a page fault. How many page faults occur?
questions.code_snippet: Reference string: 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2, 5
questions.explanation: The first three references fault, and the next 1 hits. The LRU victims for the later misses on 4, 2, and 5 are 2, 3, and 1, respectively. The pattern is F, F, F, H, F, F, F, giving 6 faults.

questions.question: A process has three initially empty frames and uses Optimal page replacement: on a fault with full frames, evict the resident page whose next use is farthest in the future; a page never used again is farthest. Break ties by the smaller page number. All references below are valid reads, and first loads count as faults. How many page faults occur?
questions.explanation: The first 7, 0, and 1 fault. On the reference to 2, neither 7 nor 1 is used again, so the tie rule evicts 1. Loading 3 later evicts 7. Loading 4 evicts 0, whose next use is later than those of 2 and 3. The later 0 faults and evicts 4. Faults occur at reference positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 11: 7 faults total.

questions.question: The current working sets below must all be resident simultaneously. Every listed private page occupies a distinct physical frame. S1 and S2 are shared read-only pages: all references to the same shared-page name use one common physical frame across processes. Ignore page-table frames and all other memory use. If nine data frames are available, how many additional frames are needed to hold these working sets?
questions.explanation: There are eight distinct private pages and two distinct shared pages, requiring 10 physical frames. Nine frames leave a shortage of one. Adding the per-process set sizes would count shared pages more than once and incorrectly suggest 13 frames are needed.

questions.question: In a single-CPU system with no concurrent accesses, the current process has a TLB entry mapping virtual page 5 to frame 12. The OS changes the page-table entry to map page 5 to resident frame 20, with unchanged readable permissions. The page-table update is complete and visible, but this system does not automatically invalidate cached TLB translations. Which action is necessary to ensure the process's next read of page 5 uses frame 20?

options.A: Make no further change; every TLB hit rechecks the frame number in the page table
options.B: Clear only the referenced/accessed bit of the updated page-table entry
options.C: Evict only the cached data for frame 12 while retaining its TLB translation
options.D: Invalidate the matching TLB entry before the next read, forcing translation from the updated page table

questions.explanation: The stale TLB entry can continue supplying frame 12 without a page-table walk. Invalidating that entry forces the next read to resolve the updated mapping to frame 20. Changing a page-table status bit or a data-cache line does not by itself remove the stipulated stale translation.

questions.question: Run the reference string below twice under FIFO page replacement: once with three frames, then independently with four frames. All frames start empty in each run. Every first load counts as a page fault, and hits do not refresh FIFO order. Which pair gives (faults with three frames, faults with four frames)?
questions.explanation: With three frames the pattern is F,F,F,F,F,F,F,H,H,F,F,H: 9 faults. With four frames it is F,F,F,F,H,H,F,F,F,F,F,F: 10 faults. This is Belady's anomaly: adding a frame can increase FIFO faults because FIFO is not a stack algorithm.

questions.question: A byte-addressable system has a four-level page table. Its 48-bit virtual address uses four 9-bit indices followed by a 12-bit offset. Every table at every level occupies one 4 KiB page and contains 512 entries. The root always exists; other tables are allocated only along paths to mapped 4 KiB pages. There are no huge pages or shared page-table pages. Exactly the ranges below are mapped. How much page-table memory is allocated, excluding data frames? Here 1 KiB = 2^10 bytes, 1 MiB = 2^20 bytes, and 1 GiB = 2^30 bytes.
questions.code_snippet:
Mapped virtual byte ranges, end-exclusive:
[0, 4 MiB)
[1 GiB, 1 GiB + 4 KiB)
[512 GiB, 512 GiB + 4 KiB)
questions.explanation: Each leaf table covers 2 MiB, so the ranges need 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 leaf tables. Their parent tables cover 1 GiB each, requiring 3 such tables for the distinct 1 GiB regions. The next level covers 512 GiB per table, requiring 2 tables: one for the first two ranges and one for the third. Including the root gives 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 table pages, or 40 KiB.

questions.question: A two-level paging system has a serial TLB lookup costing 5 ns and a TLB hit rate of 90%. Each physical-memory access costs 100 ns. A hit costs one data access after lookup. A TLB miss that does not fault costs two page-table accesses and one data access after lookup, without another lookup. Conditional on a TLB miss, the probability of a page fault is 0.001. A faulting reference costs 2 ms in total from the initial lookup through the successful retry, with no extra costs to add. TLB hits never fault, and there are no caches or overlapping operations. What is the overall mean reference time, rounded to two decimal places in ns? Use 1 ms = 1,000,000 ns.
questions.explanation: The unconditional fault probability is 0.10 * 0.001 = 0.0001, while a nonfaulting miss has probability 0.10 * 0.999 = 0.0999. Hit time is 105 ns and nonfaulting-miss time is 305 ns. Mean = 0.9 * 105 + 0.0999 * 305 + 0.0001 * 2,000,000 = 324.9695 ns, rounding to 324.97. Charging another 305 ns on each already-inclusive fault path would incorrectly round to 325.00.

questions.question: A process has two initially empty frames and uses exact LRU replacement, refreshing recency on every read or write. Loading any missing page costs 4 ms and initially makes it clean; a write then marks it dirty. Evicting a dirty page adds 6 ms of write-back before the load. Evicting a clean page costs nothing beyond the load. All I/O is serial, successful, and charged once per event. Ignore other costs and do not flush dirty pages remaining at the end. What total paging-I/O time does the trace require?
questions.code_snippet:
W1, R2, W3, R2, R1, W2, R3
Wn = write page n; Rn = read page n
questions.explanation: Faults occur on W1, the first R2, W3, R1, and R3, giving five loads. W3 evicts dirty page 1, and R1 evicts dirty page 3. The final R3 evicts clean page 1. W2 is a hit and leaves page 2 dirty but resident, so no final write-back is charged. Total = 5 * 4 + 2 * 6 = 32 ms.

questions.question: An abstract byte-addressable machine executes an 8-byte load starting at virtual address 8,190 with 4,096-byte pages. It processes page chunks in ascending address order: translate a chunk, read its data if translation succeeds, then proceed to the next chunk. Each chunk translation performs exactly one TLB lookup. A resident-page miss fills the TLB and continues without another lookup. A nonresident-page miss raises a page fault without filling the TLB or reading that chunk's data. On a fault, the handler loads the page but neither fills nor flushes the TLB; the entire instruction then restarts from its first chunk. The TLB initially is empty, holds at least two entries, and suffers no eviction. Virtual page 1 is resident; page 2 is valid but nonresident. All reads are permitted, and the handler succeeds. Through successful completion, what is the tuple (TLB misses, page faults, chunk data reads), including work discarded by the fault?
questions.explanation: Address 8,190 is page 1, offset 4,094, so the load spans pages 1 and 2. Initially page 1 misses, fills the TLB, and supplies the first chunk; page 2 misses and faults before its data is read. On restart, page 1 hits and its chunk is read again. Page 2 now is resident but still absent from the TLB, so it misses, fills, and supplies its chunk. Totals are 3 TLB misses, 1 page fault, and 3 chunk reads; there are 4 TLB lookups overall.

questions.question: Run the same address trace independently with page sizes of 4 KiB and 16 KiB. Each run uses an initially empty, fully associative 64-entry TLB with exact LRU replacement; every page has one TLB entry, and all page-table mappings are resident and readable. A 512 KiB virtual region begins at an address aligned to 16 KiB. The trace reads one byte at offsets 0, 4 KiB, 8 KiB, and so on through 508 KiB, then immediately repeats this entire sequence once. There are no other accesses, invalidations, or page faults. Which pair gives (TLB misses with 4 KiB pages, TLB misses with 16 KiB pages)? Here 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes.
questions.explanation: With 4 KiB pages the trace cycles over 128 distinct pages, exceeding the 64-entry TLB. Every reference misses in both passes, for 256 misses. With 16 KiB pages, each group of four consecutive addresses shares a translation, and the whole region uses only 32 entries. The first pass incurs 32 compulsory misses; all remaining references, including the entire second pass, hit.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: In a simplified inode-based file system, a directory entry maps a filename to an inode number, while the inode stores file metadata and data-block pointers. A regular file is renamed within its directory to a name that does not already exist. Ignoring timestamp updates, which change is sufficient without relocating the file's contents?

options.A: Allocate a new inode and copy every data block to new locations
options.B: Replace a filename field inside the file's inode and rewrite its data blocks
options.C: Change the name in the directory entry while retaining the same inode number
options.D: Replace only the file's data-block pointers while retaining the old directory entry

questions.explanation: The filename-to-inode association is stored in the directory. Renaming the entry can preserve both the inode identity and its data-block mappings; neither a replacement inode nor a copy of the file contents is required in this model.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A file uses contiguous allocation and occupies 10 consecutive disk blocks starting at physical block 120. Logical blocks are numbered from 0. Which physical block contains logical block 7?
questions.explanation: Contiguous allocation maps logical block i to start + i. Therefore logical block 7 is at physical block 120 + 7 = 127. It is within the allocated logical range 0 through 9.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A file uses linked allocation, with the next-block pointer stored inside each data block. Its first-block address is already known, but no data blocks or intermediate pointers are cached, and there is no separate FAT or index. The file has at least six blocks, numbered logically from 0. How many disk-block reads are needed to obtain the data in logical block 5, including the target-block read?
questions.explanation: The system must read logical blocks 0 through 4 to discover successive next-block addresses, then read block 5 for its data. That is five traversal reads plus one target read, or six reads total. Knowing the first address does not cache the first block's pointer.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A file uses one single-level index block of size 4 KiB, containing only 4-byte addresses of data blocks. Every data block is also 4 KiB. There are no direct pointers, extra index levels, reserved index entries, or other file-size limits. What is the maximum file-data capacity addressed by this index block? Here 1 KiB = 2^10 bytes and 1 MiB = 2^20 bytes.
questions.explanation: The index block holds 4,096/4 = 1,024 data-block addresses. These address 1,024 * 4,096 = 4,194,304 bytes of file data, or 4 MiB. The index block's own storage is metadata, not file-data capacity.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A disk head starts at cylinder 50. The pending requests below are serviced using FCFS in the listed arrival order, with no new arrivals. Head movement is the sum of absolute cylinder differences, and measurement stops when the final request is serviced. What is the total movement?
questions.code_snippet: Request queue: 60, 20, 40
questions.explanation: FCFS follows 50 -> 60 -> 20 -> 40. Movement = |60 - 50| + |20 - 60| + |40 - 20| = 10 + 40 + 20 = 70 cylinders. Net displacement does not measure total head travel.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A disk head is at cylinder 50, with the four pending requests below. SSTF selects the request with the smallest absolute cylinder distance from the current head position. Which request is selected first?
questions.code_snippet: Request queue: 20, 65, 90, 5
questions.explanation: Distances from cylinder 50 are 30, 15, 40, and 45 cylinders for requests 20, 65, 90, and 5. The unique shortest seek is to cylinder 65, regardless of its position in the arrival queue.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: An inode has 12 direct data-block pointers, one single-indirect pointer, and one double-indirect pointer. A block is 4 KiB, and each pointer occupies 4 bytes. Every indirect block contains only pointers, and a double-indirect block points to single-indirect blocks. There are no other file-size limits. How many data blocks can the inode address in total, excluding indirect metadata blocks? Here 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes.
questions.explanation: Each indirect block contains 4,096/4 = 1,024 pointers. The direct, single-indirect, and double-indirect ranges address 12, 1,024, and 1,024^2 data blocks. Their sum is 12 + 1,024 + 1,048,576 = 1,049,612.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A file's inode has 12 direct pointers followed by a single-indirect pointer. Logical data blocks are numbered from 0, and single-indirect entries are also numbered from 0. Blocks are 4,096 bytes. The inode is cached, but all indirect blocks and data blocks are uncached. A read requests the byte at decimal file offset 118,884, which is within the fully allocated file. There is no read-ahead or other I/O. Which mapping entry is used, and how many disk-block reads are needed for this byte?
questions.explanation: 118,884 = 29 * 4,096 + 100, so the byte lies in logical data block 29. Direct pointers cover blocks 0 through 11; the single-indirect entry is 29 - 12 = 17. Reading the indirect block and then the target data block requires two reads. The inode costs no read because it is cached.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A linked-allocation file contains 10,201 bytes of user data. Each allocated disk block is 1,024 bytes and reserves 4 bytes for a next-block pointer, including a null pointer in the last block. The remaining 1,020 bytes per block hold user data. Ignoring directory and inode storage, what is the pair (allocated block count, unused user-data capacity in the last block)?
questions.explanation: Ten blocks hold 10 * 1,020 = 10,200 user bytes, so one more block is needed for the final byte. Its unused user-data capacity is 1,020 - 1 = 1,019 bytes. The 44 bytes of pointers across all eleven blocks are metadata, not unused payload capacity in the last block.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A disk head starts at cylinder 53 and uses FCFS for the queue below, whose listed order is the arrival order. All requests are pending before movement starts, and no new requests arrive. Count absolute cylinder travel only and stop after servicing the final request. What is the total head movement?
questions.explanation: The successive distances are 45, 85, 146, 85, 108, 110, 59, and 2 cylinders. Their sum is 640. FCFS preserves the queue order rather than sorting requests or repeatedly choosing the nearest one.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A disk head starts at cylinder 50 and uses SSTF for the pending requests below. At every selection, equal seek distances are broken by choosing the smaller cylinder number. No new requests arrive, and movement stops after the last service. Which option gives the service order and total head movement?
questions.code_snippet: Request queue: 10, 30, 70, 90
questions.explanation: Initially 30 and 70 are both 20 cylinders away, so the tie rule selects 30. From there, 10 is nearest, followed by 70 and 90. Travel is 20 + 20 + 60 + 20 = 120 cylinders. Choosing 70 first would violate the stated tie rule even though that alternative also travels 120 cylinders.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: Compare independent SCAN and LOOK runs on cylinders 0 through 199. The head starts at 50 moving toward larger cylinder numbers, with exactly the pending requests below and no new arrivals. SCAN goes to endpoint 199 before reversing to service lower requests; LOOK reverses at the highest pending request instead. Both service encountered requests and stop immediately after the last request is serviced. What is the pair (SCAN movement, LOOK movement)? Count all physical travel in cylinders.
questions.code_snippet: Pending requests: 10, 20, 70, 90
questions.explanation: SCAN travels 50 -> 199 -> 10, covering (199 - 50) + (199 - 10) = 338 cylinders. LOOK travels 50 -> 90 -> 10, covering (90 - 50) + (90 - 10) = 120. Neither run continues toward cylinder 0 after servicing the final request at 10.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A disk has cylinders 0 through 199 and uses C-SCAN, servicing requests only while moving toward larger cylinder numbers. The head starts at 50 with the pending requests below. After reaching 199 it returns directly to 0 without servicing requests during the return, then resumes upward service. Charge the full 199-cylinder return movement, allow no new arrivals, and stop when the last request is serviced. What is the total head movement?
questions.code_snippet: Pending requests: 10, 20, 70, 90
questions.explanation: The path is 50 -> 70 -> 90 -> 199 -> 0 -> 10 -> 20. Total movement = (199 - 50) + (199 - 0) + (20 - 0) = 149 + 199 + 20 = 368 cylinders. The return is charged even though it services no requests, and the run ends at 20 rather than continuing to an endpoint.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A disk head starts at cylinder 80 moving toward smaller cylinder numbers and uses LOOK. All requests below are initially pending, and no new ones arrive. LOOK reverses at the lowest pending request in its initial direction, not at a disk endpoint, and stops after the final service. What is the total movement?
questions.code_snippet: Pending requests: 10, 50, 90, 160
questions.explanation: The service order is 50, 10, 90, 160. Travel is (80 - 50) + (50 - 10) + (90 - 10) + (160 - 90) = 30 + 40 + 80 + 70 = 220 cylinders. The initial downward direction matters; starting upward would give 230.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: An SSTF disk head starts at cylinder 50 with an old request at 190 and a request at 49. Whenever the head services 49, a new request at 50 arrives before the next selection; whenever it services 50, a new request at 49 arrives before the next selection. This arrival pattern continues forever, with no other requests. SSTF always selects the currently nearest pending request. What happens to the request at 190?

options.A: It must be serviced after at most two nearby requests because it arrived first
options.B: It is serviced on the next upward sweep because SSTF requires an endpoint visit
options.C: It is serviced next, while all alternating requests remain unserved
options.D: It can starve indefinitely while the head continues servicing requests at 49 and 50

questions.explanation: At each selection a pending request is only one cylinder away, while 190 is at least 140 cylinders away. SSTF therefore keeps choosing the alternating nearby requests. It imposes neither FIFO order nor SCAN-style sweeps, so this legal infinite arrival stream starves the older distant request.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: Compare two independent file-system designs: pure contiguous allocation and linked allocation. In each design, a file currently occupies blocks 100 through 103 in order and must append one block. Block 104 belongs to another file, blocks 200 through 205 are free, and no other blocks are free. Sufficient metadata space is available. Contiguous allocation does not support multiple extents. Without relocating any existing data block of this file, can the append succeed under (contiguous allocation, linked allocation)?
questions.explanation: Contiguous allocation needs block 104 to extend the current extent in place, but that block is unavailable. Moving the file to a larger free run would violate the no-relocation requirement. Linked allocation can append block 200, update the old tail's next pointer, and retain all existing data-block locations.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: An inode has 12 direct pointers, one single-indirect pointer, and one double-indirect pointer. Blocks are 1 KiB and pointers are 4 bytes; every indirect block holds only pointers. A non-sparse file is exactly 525 KiB, and its data fills logical blocks in order, using direct pointers first, then the single-indirect range, then the double-indirect range. Allocate indirect blocks only when needed. How many total disk blocks hold this file's data and indirect metadata, excluding the inode itself and directory storage? Here 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes.
questions.explanation: There are 525 data blocks, and an indirect block holds 1,024/4 = 256 pointers. After 12 direct and 256 single-indirect data blocks, 257 data blocks remain in the double-indirect range. Metadata comprises one single-indirect block, one double-indirect root, and ceil(257/256) = two indirect children. Total = 525 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 529 blocks. The extra child is required even though it holds only one data-block pointer.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: A SCAN disk has cylinders 0 through 199. At time 0 the head is at 50, moving upward, with requests at 80 and 20 pending. The head moves continuously at one cylinder per ms; service time is zero. A request arriving at a cylinder still ahead in the current sweep is serviced when encountered; one arriving after the head has passed its cylinder waits for the return sweep. The head reverses only at disk endpoints while requests remain. Additional requests arrive as shown, and there are no others. At what absolute time is the request that arrives at cylinder 60 serviced?
questions.code_snippet:
Arrival time | Requested cylinder
15 ms        | 60
100 ms       | 180
