questions.explanation: At time 15 the head is at 65, so the new request at 60 has missed the upward sweep. The head services 80 at time 30. At time 100 it is at 150, so the new request at 180 is serviced on the same sweep at time 130. SCAN reaches endpoint 199 at time 149, then needs 199 - 60 = 139 ms to return to 60. The requested absolute service time is 149 + 139 = 288 ms, rather than its waiting time of 273 ms.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: Compare independent SSTF and FCFS runs for the queue below. All four requests arrive at time 0, when the head is at cylinder 50. Each service takes 2 ms plus 0.1 ms per cylinder traveled from the previous head position; these costs are serial and include every service cost. SSTF selects by cylinder distance only and breaks ties toward the smaller cylinder. FCFS uses the listed order. No new requests arrive. Define response time here as arrival-to-service-completion time. What is the pair (mean response time under SSTF, mean response time under FCFS)?
questions.code_snippet: Request queue: 10, 90, 20, 80
questions.explanation: SSTF serves 20, 10, 80, 90, traveling 30, 10, 70, 10 cylinders. Service durations are 5, 3, 9, 3 ms, giving completion times 5, 8, 17, 20 and mean 50/4 = 12.5 ms. FCFS travels 40, 80, 70, 60 cylinders, with durations 6, 10, 9, 8 ms and completion times 6, 16, 25, 33, averaging 80/4 = 20.0 ms. Averaging individual service durations instead of cumulative completion times would answer a different question.

questions.subpart_name: Storage Systems, File Systems & Disk Scheduling
questions.question: In a simplified inode-based file system, /a and /b are hard links to regular-file inode I, while /c names a different regular-file inode J. Initially there are no open descriptors. All operations below succeed in one file system. rename replaces the destination directory entry atomically without changing the file identity of existing open descriptors. unlink removes only the named hard link. An inode's data blocks become reclaimable only when both its hard-link count and open-descriptor count are zero; there are no other references or deferred-reclamation rules. Immediately after the trace, which inode's data blocks are reclaimable?
questions.code_snippet:
fdI = open('/a')
fdJ = open('/c')
unlink('/a')
rename('/b', '/c')
close(fdI)
unlink('/c')
// fdJ remains open

options.A: Both I and J, because neither has a remaining directory name
options.B: Neither I nor J, because both still have an open descriptor
options.C: Only I; J remains referenced by fdJ
options.D: Only J; I remains referenced by the renamed /c directory entry

questions.explanation: I starts with two hard links. Removing /a leaves one; renaming /b to /c retains that one link while removing J's only link. fdJ still refers to J. Closing fdI leaves I with no open descriptor, and the final unlink removes I's last link, making I's blocks reclaimable. J has zero links but one open descriptor, so its blocks are retained.

questions.question: For the relation instance below, which listed functional dependency is violated? Attribute values are atomic and non-NULL.
questions.code_snippet:
Employee | Department | Head
E1       | D1         | H1
E2       | D1         | H2
E3       | D2         | H3
questions.explanation: The two D1 rows have different Head values, violating Department -> Head. Employee and Head values are each unique in this instance, so each of the other listed dependencies holds for these rows. An instance satisfying an FD does not by itself prove that FD is a schema constraint.

questions.question: For the schema and complete FD set below, what is the attribute closure A+?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->C
questions.explanation: Start with A, obtain B using A->B, then C using B->C. No dependency derives D, so the closure is exactly {A,B,C}.

questions.question: For the atomic relation below, which option lists all candidate keys? Assume the given FDs and their logical consequences are the only constraints relevant to keys.
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C)
FDs: A->B; A->C
questions.explanation: A determines every attribute and is minimal. AB and AC are superkeys but are not candidate keys because they properly contain A. Neither B nor C can derive A.

questions.question: Which listed attribute set is a superkey but is not a candidate key under exactly the FDs below?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->C
questions.explanation: AD is a candidate key because A derives B and C while D must be supplied. ABD also determines all attributes, but B is unnecessary, so ABD is a nonminimal superkey.

questions.question: All values are atomic. Enrollment has exactly the FDs below, where (Student,Course) is its only candidate key. What is its highest normal form among the listed choices?
questions.code_snippet:
Enrollment(Student,Course,StudentName,Grade)
FDs: Student->StudentName; Student,Course->Grade
questions.explanation: StudentName is nonprime and depends on Student, a proper subset of the composite candidate key. This partial dependency violates 2NF. Atomic values establish 1NF, so 1NF is the highest listed form.

questions.question: A Phone column has a declared domain of one phone number, but Person stores a set of phone numbers in each Phone cell. Which redesign removes this repeating group while retaining every person-phone association?

options.A: Keep one row per person and serialize the set into the same Phone cell
options.B: Keep the set-valued cell and add a surrogate row identifier
options.C: Create Phone1, Phone2, and Phone3 columns and reject any fourth phone
options.D: Use PersonPhone(PersonID,Phone), with one phone number per row and key (PersonID,Phone)

questions.explanation: One association per row makes Phone conform to its single-number domain and allows arbitrarily many numbers. Serializing the list, fixing a repeating-column limit, or adding an identifier does not normalize the stated repeating group.

questions.question: For R(A,B,C), which FD is trivial solely by the definition of a trivial dependency, without using any additional constraints?
questions.explanation: An FD X->Y is trivial when Y is a subset of X. A is already contained in AB; each other option places an attribute on the right that is absent from its left side.

questions.question: All values are atomic, and the following are the complete FD constraints. What is the highest normal form of R?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B)
FDs: A->B; B->A
questions.explanation: A and B are each candidate keys. Every nontrivial FD has a superkey determinant, satisfying BCNF, the strongest of the listed forms.

questions.question: All values are atomic. EmployeeID is the only candidate key, and the complete nontrivial FD basis is shown. What is the highest normal form?
questions.code_snippet:
R(EmployeeID,Department,Manager)
FDs: EmployeeID->Department; Department->Manager
questions.explanation: The single-attribute key has no proper nonempty subset causing a partial dependency, so 2NF holds. Department is not a superkey and Manager is nonprime; Department->Manager violates 3NF through a transitive dependency from EmployeeID.

questions.question: For the complete FD basis below, what is A+? Apply dependencies until no additional attributes can be derived.
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D,E,F)
FDs: A->BC; C->D; BD->E; E->F
questions.explanation: A supplies B and C. C supplies D, making both B and D available for BD->E. E then supplies F. Thus every attribute belongs to A+.

questions.question: For R below, which option lists exactly all candidate keys?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->A; C->D
questions.explanation: C never occurs on a right-hand side, so every key includes C. Either A or B is needed to obtain the interchangeable pair A,B. AC and BC each derive all four attributes and are minimal; ABC is not minimal.

questions.question: How many distinct superkeys, counting different attribute subsets separately, does this schema have?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->A; C->D
questions.explanation: A superkey must contain C and at least one of A or B. There are three nonempty choices from {A,B}: A, B, or AB. D may independently be present or absent, giving 3 * 2 = 6 superkeys.

questions.question: An attribute is prime if it occurs in at least one candidate key. Which option lists exactly the prime attributes of this schema?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->A; C->D
questions.explanation: The candidate keys are AC and BC. Their union is {A,B,C}; D appears in neither minimal key and is therefore nonprime.

questions.question: All values are atomic. Under exactly the FDs below, what is the highest normal form of R?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C)
FDs: AB->C; C->B
questions.explanation: The candidate keys are AB and AC, making all three attributes prime. C->B is allowed by 3NF because B is prime, but it violates BCNF because C+ = {B,C}, so C is not a superkey.

questions.question: All values are atomic. Determine the highest normal form under the complete FD basis below; no candidate key is supplied in advance.
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: AB->C; B->C; C->D
questions.explanation: A and B are absent from all right-hand sides, so the only candidate key is AB. B, a proper subset of that key, determines nonprime C and D. This violates 2NF, leaving 1NF as the highest form.

questions.question: Which listed dependency demonstrates a BCNF violation in the following schema? Consider all FDs implied by the given basis.
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->C; C->D
questions.explanation: B+ = {B,C,D}, which lacks A, so B is not a superkey; B->C is nontrivial and violates BCNF. A and AB are superkeys, while CD->C is trivial.

questions.question: For the complete FD basis below, classify the decomposition into AB and AC. Lossless means every legal original relation equals the join of its projections; dependency preservation means the projected FDs jointly imply the original FDs.
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C)
FDs: A->B
Decomposition: R1(A,B), R2(A,C)
questions.explanation: The intersection is A, and A->AB, so the binary decomposition is lossless. A->B can be enforced within AB, preserving the complete FD basis.

questions.question: Under exactly F = {A->B}, classify the decomposition of R(A,B,C) into AB and BC.
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C)
FDs: A->B
Decomposition: R1(A,B), R2(B,C)
questions.explanation: The intersection B determines neither AB nor BC, so the binary lossless-join criterion fails. The original A->B remains enforceable in AB, so the decomposition nevertheless preserves dependencies.

questions.question: Under exactly the FDs below, classify the decomposition into AC and BC.
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C)
FDs: AB->C; C->B
Decomposition: R1(A,C), R2(B,C)
questions.explanation: The intersection C determines BC, establishing losslessness. The nontrivial projected constraint is C->B in BC; AC has no nontrivial FD. Their union cannot derive AB->C, so dependency preservation fails.

questions.question: A decomposition produces AB, BC, and CD under the FDs below. Can enforcing the projected FDs within these tables guarantee the original consequence A->D, without a cross-table FD check?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->C; C->D
Decomposition: R1(A,B), R2(B,C), R3(C,D)

options.A: No; transitivity cannot be used across projected FD sets
options.B: Yes; the locally enforced chain A->B, B->C, C->D implies A->D
options.C: No; A and D must occur together in one component
options.D: Yes, but only if every component uses A as its primary key

questions.explanation: Dependency preservation uses the logical closure of the union of projected FDs. The three local dependencies imply A->D by transitivity, even though A and D never appear together in a component.

questions.question: Which option is an equivalent minimal cover with singleton right-hand sides for the FD set below? Minimal means no FD or left-side attribute can be removed while preserving equivalence.
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C)
FDs: A->BC; B->C; A->B; AB->C
questions.explanation: Split A->BC into A->B and A->C. A->C and AB->C follow from A->B and B->C, so they are redundant. Neither remaining dependency can be removed or have its singleton determinant reduced.

questions.question: Which single FD can be removed from this basis without changing its closure?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D,E)
FDs: A->B; B->C; A->C; CD->E
questions.explanation: A->C follows from A->B and B->C. Removing any of the other three loses a consequence: A could no longer derive B, B could no longer derive C, or CD could no longer derive E, respectively.

questions.question: A standard dependency-preserving 3NF synthesis has produced AB and CD from the FD basis below. Neither component contains a candidate key of the original schema. Which listed relation should be added in the synthesis key-containment step?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->A; C->D
Current components: R1(A,B), R2(C,D)

options.B: No additional relation is needed for the key-containment step

questions.explanation: The original candidate keys are AC and BC. Adding AC supplies a relation containing a complete candidate key, which makes the standard synthesis lossless. AD and BD cannot derive C and therefore are not keys.

questions.question: Project the full FD closure of the original schema onto attributes {A,C,D}. Which listed nontrivial FD must hold in that projection?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->C
Projected schema: S(A,C,D)
questions.explanation: A->C is implied by A->B and B->C, and both A and C survive projection. Projection includes implied dependencies, not just the syntactically listed FDs whose attributes all remain. No listed FD can derive A from C or D.

questions.question: Under exactly the FDs below, how many candidate keys does R have? Count minimal keys only.
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D,E)
FDs: AB->C; C->A; BC->D; D->E; E->B
questions.explanation: The six candidate keys are AB, AD, AE, BC, CD, and CE. Each pair closes to all five attributes; no singleton does. Every other pair fails, and every three-attribute set contains one of those six keys, so no larger minimal key exists.

questions.question: All values are atomic. What is the highest normal form under this complete FD basis?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: AB->C; C->D; D->A
questions.explanation: The candidate keys are AB, BC, and BD, so every attribute is prime. Consequently every implied singleton-right-side nontrivial FD satisfies 3NF. C and D are not superkeys because neither derives B, so C->D and D->A prevent BCNF.

questions.question: R has no nontrivial FD constraints. For the displayed legal instance, which tuple is absent from R but appears in the natural join of its projections onto AB, BC, and AC?
questions.explanation: AB contains (0,0) from the first row, BC contains (0,0) from the third, and AC contains (0,0) from the second. Those projections join to (0,0,0), which was absent. Thus even all three pairwise projections can lose the original three-way association.

questions.question: Classify the three-component decomposition below under the complete FD basis, considering projected dependencies and losslessness of the entire decomposition.
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->C; CD->A
Decomposition: R1(A,B), R2(B,C), R3(A,D)
questions.explanation: AB and BC reconstruct the ABC projection losslessly because B->C. Combining ABC with AD is lossless because their intersection A determines ABC. However, the projected FDs are generated by A->B and B->C; AD has no nontrivial projected FD. They cannot derive CD->A, so that dependency is not preserved.

questions.question: Compare the two decompositions below under the full FD closure. Which statement is correct?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->C; C->D
D1: AB, BC, CD
D2: AB, AC, AD

options.A: Both are lossless BCNF decompositions and both preserve all original dependencies
options.B: D2 preserves all dependencies, but D1 loses A->D
options.C: Both are lossless BCNF decompositions, but only D1 preserves all original dependencies
options.D: D1 is lossless, but D2 is lossy because its components share only A

questions.explanation: Every component has a key determinant, so both decompositions are in BCNF. D1 is lossless by the dependency chain and preserves each original FD locally. D2 is lossless because A determines all attributes and is shared across its components, but its projected A->B, A->C, and A->D do not imply B->C or C->D.

questions.question: When testing dependency preservation for the decomposition below, which conclusion correctly uses the full projected FD sets rather than only the explicitly written FDs?
questions.code_snippet:
R(A,B,C,D)
FDs: A->B; B->C; C->A; C->D
Decomposition: R1(A,B), R2(B,C), R3(A,D)

options.A: The decomposition preserves dependencies only after adding a separate CD relation
options.B: C->D is lost because no component contains both C and D
options.C: All original FDs are preserved; projected C->B, B->A, and A->D imply C->D
options.D: C->A is lost because no component contains both C and A

questions.explanation: A, B, and C determine each other under the original basis. Projection therefore includes B->A in AB and C->B in BC, as well as A->D in AD. Their union recovers the cycle A->B->C->A and derives C->D via C->B->A->D, preserving the entire original basis.

questions.question: A bank transfer transaction debits account A, but a failure occurs before it credits account B. Recovery removes the debit so that neither update remains. Which ACID property directly requires this all-or-nothing outcome?

options.C: Consistency of a declared interest-rate formula

questions.explanation: Atomicity requires a transaction to take effect completely or not at all. Since the transfer did not commit, recovery must remove its partial debit rather than leave only half of the transfer.

questions.question: A transaction commits and the database acknowledges success. A power failure follows before the changed data page is written to its final disk location. Recovery reconstructs the committed change from durable logging. Which ACID property is being fulfilled?

options.D: Consistency of every application business rule

questions.explanation: Durability requires acknowledged committed effects to survive the failure model the system promises to tolerate. It does not require every data page to have reached its final location at commit if durable recovery information can reconstruct the change.

questions.question: A transaction attempts to insert an order referencing a nonexistent customer. The database rejects it to preserve a declared foreign-key invariant. Which ACID property describes the requirement that committed transactions preserve declared integrity constraints?

options.A: Atomicity alone, regardless of integrity constraints
options.B: Durability alone, regardless of integrity constraints
options.C: Isolation alone, regardless of integrity constraints

questions.explanation: Consistency requires committed transactions to take a valid database state to another valid state under its declared constraints. Enforcing the foreign key preserves that invariant; it does not validate arbitrary business rules that were never expressed or correctly implemented.

questions.question: In the trace below, T2 reads the value written by T1 before T1 commits, and T1 later aborts. What anomaly has already occurred? r means read, w means write, and a means abort.

options.A: Phantom read involving a changed result-set membership
options.B: Nonrepeatable read requiring two reads by T2
options.C: A lost update requiring T2 to overwrite X

questions.explanation: T2 observed an uncommitted value that T1 subsequently rolls back. That is a dirty read. The trace contains neither a second read nor a predicate query or a T2 write needed for the other listed anomalies.

questions.question: Two operations conflict for conflict-serializability analysis only when they belong to different transactions, access the same item, and at least one is a write. Which pair conflicts?
questions.explanation: The read and write on X belong to different transactions and cannot generally be swapped without changing observed behavior. Two reads, operations on different items, or two operations of one transaction do not form an inter-transaction conflict pair.

questions.question: Ignoring commits and assuming the shown data operations are complete, what serial transaction order is conflict-equivalent to the trace below?
questions.explanation: The write by T1 precedes the conflicting read by T2, giving the precedence edge T1->T2. The graph is acyclic and permits only the serial order T1 then T2.

questions.question: Under basic two-phase locking, a transaction may acquire or upgrade locks during its growing phase but may not acquire or upgrade any lock after releasing one. Which trace violates this rule? S and X denote successful shared and exclusive acquisitions; all locks shown are otherwise compatible with the environment.

options.B: S(A); upgrade A to X; unlock(A)

questions.explanation: The violating trace starts its shrinking phase at unlock(A) and then acquires S(B). The other traces finish all acquisitions and upgrades before their first release.

questions.question: An immediate-update database uses write-ahead logging. An uncommitted transaction has modified a page, and the buffer manager wants to write that page to disk under a steal policy. What must become durable first?

options.A: The log records describing the page updates through the page LSN
options.B: Only the page itself; its update records can be forced later
options.C: The transaction commit record, even though the transaction has not committed
options.D: Every dirty page in the database

questions.explanation: WAL requires recovery information for an update to be durable before the corresponding modified page reaches disk. A steal policy permits uncommitted data pages on disk, so the transaction need not already have a commit record.

questions.question: A no-force database has durably logged a transaction commit, but one of that transaction's changed pages may still contain its old disk value when a crash occurs. What recovery capability addresses this situation?

options.A: Requiring every reader to reissue the committed transaction
options.B: UNDO of the committed transaction as if it had aborted
options.C: Discarding the commit record because the data page was not forced
options.D: REDO of committed updates from durable recovery information

questions.explanation: No-force allows a commit without flushing all changed pages. Durable logs must therefore support reapplying committed changes that did not reach their data pages. Undoing an acknowledged commit would violate durability.

questions.question: For the complete data-operation schedule below, which serial order is conflict-equivalent? Analyze every conflict on the same item between different transactions.
questions.explanation: The conflicts on X require T1->T2, and the conflict on Y requires T2->T3. These edges form the chain T1->T2->T3, which admits only that serial order.

questions.question: Is the following complete data-operation schedule conflict-serializable?

options.A: Yes; its only serial order is T2,T1
options.B: Yes; both serial orders are possible because X and Y are different items
options.C: No; the graph contains T1->T2 and T2->T1
options.D: Yes; its only serial order is T1,T2

questions.explanation: The write/read conflict on X gives T1->T2. The write/read conflict on Y gives T2->T1. A cycle across different items is still a precedence-graph cycle, so no conflict-equivalent serial schedule exists.

questions.question: How many serial transaction orders are conflict-equivalent to this complete schedule? Count each permutation of T1,T2,T3 separately.
questions.explanation: The graph has T1->T3 and T2->T3, with no edge between T1 and T2. T3 must be last, while T1 and T2 can occur in either order: T1,T2,T3 or T2,T1,T3.

questions.question: Which graph property correctly determines conflict serializability for the complete schedule below?

options.A: It is serializable because no single item is accessed by all three transactions
options.B: It is not conflict-serializable because T1->T2->T3->T1 is a cycle
options.C: It is serializable because the graph has no two-vertex cycle
options.D: It is serializable in order T1,T2,T3

questions.explanation: The three items create edges T1->T2, T2->T3, and T3->T1. A cycle of length three suffices to rule out conflict serializability; a two-vertex cycle is not necessary.

questions.question: Classify the schedule into the strongest applicable category among the mutually exclusive options. r2(X) reads from w1(X); c means commit and a means abort. A recoverable schedule never commits a reader before its source transaction commits.
questions.explanation: T2 commits after reading T1's uncommitted write, but T1 aborts without ever committing. This violates recoverability, so none of the stronger categories can apply.

questions.question: Classify the schedule into the strongest applicable category. r2(X) reads from w1(X). Strict schedules forbid another transaction from reading or overwriting an uncommitted write; cascadeless schedules forbid only the uncommitted reads.
questions.explanation: T2 waits until T1 commits before committing itself, so the read-from dependency is recoverable. However, T2 reads before c1, making the schedule neither cascadeless nor strict.

questions.question: Classify this write-only schedule into the strongest applicable category. Both writes are blind writes, there are no reads, and strict means no other transaction may read or overwrite an item written by an unfinished transaction.
questions.explanation: With no reads, the no-dirty-read requirement is satisfied vacuously, so the schedule is cascadeless and recoverable. But w2 overwrites T1's uncommitted write before c1, violating strictness.

questions.question: Use these conventions: basic 2PL forbids lock acquisition after any release; strict 2PL additionally holds every X lock through commit/abort; rigorous 2PL holds both S and X locks through commit/abort. All acquisitions below succeed. Which protocol classification is correct?
questions.code_snippet: S1(A); X1(B); unlock1(A); c1; unlock1(B)

options.A: Allowed by both strict and rigorous 2PL
options.B: Allowed by strict 2PL, but not by rigorous 2PL
options.C: Allowed by rigorous 2PL but not strict 2PL
options.D: Disallowed by both because strict 2PL also holds every S lock until commit

questions.explanation: All acquisitions precede the first release, and the X lock on B survives through commit, satisfying strict 2PL as defined. Releasing S(A) before commit violates the stronger rigorous rule.

questions.question: A lock manager allows concurrent S locks but grants X only when no other transaction holds any lock on that item. Upgrades retain the existing S lock while waiting. In the trace below, what happens if there is no timeout, abort, or deadlock recovery?
questions.code_snippet: S1(X) granted; S2(X) granted; T1 requests upgrade to X(X); T2 requests upgrade to X(X)

options.A: T1 upgrades immediately because it requested first despite T2's S lock
options.B: Basic 2PL automatically aborts T2 and therefore prevents this deadlock
options.C: Both upgrades wait indefinitely because each transaction retains an S lock blocking the other
options.D: T2 upgrades immediately because upgrades ignore existing shared holders

questions.explanation: Each upgrade requires the other shared holder to release its lock. Both retain those locks while waiting, creating a deadlock. Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability of completed schedules, not freedom from lock deadlocks.

questions.question: All three transactions remain uncommitted. r2(X) reads T1's value, and r3(Y) reads T2's value. If the system prevents any transaction from committing based on an aborted source, which additional transactions must abort when T1 aborts?
questions.explanation: T2 used T1's aborted value, so it must roll back. T3 used T2's subsequently invalidated value, so the rollback cascades to T3. The dependency is transitive, not limited to direct readers of T1.

questions.question: A simple immediate-update UNDO/REDO system starts from a durable checkpoint with A=100 and B=200. The durable log below is complete, and a crash follows. Recovery redoes committed updates and undoes uncommitted updates using before-images. There are no other transactions or writes. What final values must recovery establish?
questions.code_snippet:
<T1, A, old=100, new=130>
<T2, B, old=200, new=170>
<COMMIT T1>
<CRASH>
questions.explanation: T1 committed, so its A=130 must survive even if redo is needed. T2 did not commit, so B must return to its old value 200 even if the dirty value 170 reached disk.

questions.question: A database permits both steal and no-force buffer management. It uses immediate updates and durable logs sufficient to recover from a crash. Which pair of capabilities is required in the general case?

options.A: Neither UNDO nor REDO, because forcing the log forces all data pages
options.B: UNDO only, because no-force guarantees committed pages are on disk
options.C: UNDO for uncommitted changes that reached disk, and REDO for committed changes that did not
options.D: REDO only, because steal forbids uncommitted pages on disk

questions.explanation: Steal allows uncommitted data to reach disk, requiring undo or an equivalent mechanism. No-force allows committed data to be missing from disk, requiring redo or an equivalent mechanism. Forcing log records is not the same as forcing data pages.

questions.question: At checkpoint C, all active transactions have finished and every committed dirty page is forced to disk before the checkpoint completes. T1 committed before C. T2 starts after C, changes X, and commits. T3 starts after C, changes a different item Y, and is active at the crash. In a simple UNDO/REDO recovery with a complete durable post-C log, which transaction work is needed?

options.A: Skip every transaction because a checkpoint eliminates all later recovery
options.B: REDO T1 and T2, and treat T3 as committed
options.C: REDO T2 and UNDO T3; no T1 recovery work is needed
options.D: UNDO T2 and T3 because both started after C

questions.explanation: The quiescent, forced checkpoint makes T1's earlier committed state durable. T2's post-checkpoint committed update may need redo under no-force, while T3's uncommitted change may need undo under steal. The checkpoint does not cover later work.

questions.question: A fuzzy checkpoint neither stops active transactions nor forces all dirty pages. T1 updated X before the checkpoint, remains active through it, and is still uncommitted at the crash. The checkpoint records T1 as active but does not itself contain X's before-image. Why can the system not simply discard every pre-checkpoint log record?

options.A: A checkpoint automatically commits T1, so its commit record must be discarded instead
options.B: Every pre-checkpoint transaction must be replayed as uncommitted regardless of status
options.C: The checkpoint necessarily contains an entire clean copy of X, making older records irrelevant
options.D: T1 may need a pre-checkpoint update record and its before-image to undo its earlier change

questions.explanation: An active transaction can span a fuzzy checkpoint. If its earlier uncommitted update reached disk, recovery still needs enough earlier log information to undo it. Recording an active transaction ID is not a replacement for the required before-image or equivalent undo information.

questions.question: For the complete write-only schedule below, classify both conflict serializability and view serializability. View equivalence preserves reads-from relations, reads of initial values, and each item's final writer. There are no reads here.
questions.explanation: The writes create edges T1->T2 and T2->T1, so conflict serializability fails. With no reads, only the final writer matters; serial order T2,T1 ends with T1 writing X and is view-equivalent. Blind writes make this separation possible.

questions.question: Classify the complete schedule below under both conflict and view serializability. The first read sees the initial value of X. In a candidate serial schedule, each transaction keeps its own internal operation order.
questions.explanation: The read/write conflict gives T1->T2, while the later write/write conflict gives T2->T1. For view equivalence, T1's initial-value read requires T1 before T2, but final writer T1 requires T2 before T1. Neither serial order satisfies both constraints.

questions.question: Which serial order is view-equivalent to this complete schedule? r3(X) reads the value of the second w1(X). View equivalence must preserve that source transaction and the final writer of each item; each transaction retains its own operation order.
questions.explanation: X's final writer is T1, forcing T2 before T1 in a serial schedule. T3 must read X from T1, forcing T1 before T3. Thus T2,T1,T3 is the only listed view-equivalent order, although T1 and T2 form a conflict cycle in the original trace.

questions.question: Every read requires an S or X lock held for that operation, and every write requires an X lock. Locks may be acquired early, but basic 2PL forbids any acquisition or upgrade after any release. Does a placement of lock/unlock operations exist that produces exactly the data-operation order below?

options.A: No, because the precedence graph contains a cycle
options.B: No, although the schedule is conflict-serializable in order T3,T1,T2
options.C: Yes; every conflict-serializable operation schedule can be generated by basic 2PL
options.D: Yes; T1 may release A and subsequently acquire B under basic 2PL

questions.explanation: Conflicts impose T3->T1->T2, so the schedule is conflict-serializable. But T1 must release its A lock before w2(A), starting its shrinking phase. It must acquire its B lock before that release to satisfy 2PL, then retain it until r1(B). Such a held B lock prevents the intervening w3(B). Therefore this exact schedule cannot arise under basic 2PL.

questions.question: Initially A=10 and B=20. Strict 2PL holds X locks through termination. T1 locks A and writes A=11; T2 locks B and writes B=22. T1 then requests a read lock on B, while T2 requests a read lock on A, creating deadlock. Recovery aborts T2, restores B using its before-image, and only then releases T2's locks. T1 resumes, reads B, sets A to its current own value plus the B it reads, and commits. With no other transactions, what final values remain?
questions.explanation: T2's abort restores B from 22 to 20 before T1 can read it. T1 still sees its own A=11, so it writes 11 + 20 = 31 and commits. Strict locking prevents T1 from consuming the aborted B=22 value.

questions.question: Use the explicit redo rule below: scan candidate update records in increasing LSN order, redo a record only if its LSN exceeds the target page's current pageLSN, and set pageLSN to that LSN after redo. All listed transactions committed, and no undo is needed. On disk, P has pageLSN 40 and Q has pageLSN 10. Which candidate LSNs are actually redone?
questions.code_snippet:
LSN | Page | Redo value
20  | P    | 5
30  | Q    | 12
40  | P    | 9
50  | Q    | 15
questions.explanation: P already reflects LSN 40, so both P records at 20 and 40 are skipped. Q starts at 10, so LSN 30 is redone and advances it to 30; LSN 50 is then redone and advances it to 50. Comparing each record to the current target page's LSN makes redo repeatable.

questions.question: A restartable UNDO/REDO model uses compensation log records (CLRs). T1 made the two X updates below but never committed; T2 committed Y=220. First recovery undid T1's LSN 20 and forced CLR 50, whose redo sets X=110 and whose nextToUndo is 10, then crashed before undoing LSN 10. No recovery data-page writes reached disk, so disk values again are X=120 and Y=200. On the second restart, first redo T2's committed update and every durable CLR, then resume T1 undo at the CLR's nextToUndo. After recovery finishes, what values remain?
questions.code_snippet:
LSN 10: T1, X, old=100, new=110
LSN 20: T1, X, old=110, new=120
LSN 30: T2, Y, old=200, new=220
LSN 40: COMMIT T2
LSN 50: CLR for T1, redo X=110, nextToUndo=10
questions.explanation: Second-restart redo restores T2's Y=220 and reapplies CLR 50 to set X=110. The CLR identifies LSN 10 as the remaining undo work; its before-image restores X=100. The already compensated LSN 20 is not undone again, and the uncommitted T1 effects disappear despite the recovery crash.

questions.question: In this B+ tree model, all record entries are stored in leaves, while internal nodes contain separator keys and child pointers only. A lookup finds its search key among an internal node's separators. What must happen to retrieve the record?

options.A: Continue through the appropriate child until the matching leaf entry is reached
options.B: Declare the record absent because internal keys cannot also occur at leaves
options.C: Scan every leaf because matching a separator makes child selection impossible
options.D: Return a complete record directly from that separator

questions.explanation: An internal separator guides routing but is not itself the record entry in the stated B+ tree model. The lookup must reach the leaf. Equality is routed according to the tree's separator convention.

questions.question: A B+ tree defines order m as the maximum number of child pointers in an internal node. Each internal node with c children has c-1 separator keys. If m=5, what is the maximum number of separators in such a node?
questions.explanation: A node with the maximum five children has five minus one = four separator keys. Definitions of order vary, so the question explicitly fixes the maximum-child convention.

questions.question: A table stores one physical copy of its rows. A clustered index determines the physical row ordering in that copy, while non-clustered indexes store separate search structures. Two proposed clustering keys induce different row orders. How many of these independent physical clustering orders can that one row copy simultaneously have?

options.A: As many as there are non-clustered indexes
options.B: One per indexed column, without another row copy

questions.explanation: A single physical row sequence cannot simultaneously follow two different orders. Multiple non-clustered indexes may coexist because they are separate structures, but another independent physical clustering order would need another organization or copy.

questions.question: A non-clustered index stores key K and included column V in its leaf entries. A query selects only K and V and filters only on K. Assume index entries supply all required visibility and permission information, and ignore other checks. Is fetching base-table data pages necessary for the returned column values?

options.A: Yes; every included column is stored only in the base table
options.B: No; the index covers all requested columns
options.C: No; because every non-clustered index physically reorders the base table
options.D: Yes; a non-clustered index can never supply selected column values

questions.explanation: Both selected values and the predicate key are present in the index, enabling an index-only retrieval under the stated assumptions. Coverage, not physical clustering, determines whether base-table values are needed here.

questions.question: Each Employee belongs to exactly one Department, and a Department may have many Employees or none. DepartmentID and EmployeeID are their respective keys. Which mapping directly enforces the Employee-to-Department association while permitting many employees in one department?

options.A: Put one EmployeeID scalar foreign key in Department and no reference in Employee
options.B: Store the department name only inside Employee without a foreign key
options.C: Put a UNIQUE DepartmentID foreign key in Employee
options.D: Put a NOT NULL DepartmentID foreign key in Employee, without a UNIQUE constraint on that foreign key

questions.explanation: The foreign key belongs on the many side. NOT NULL enforces each employee's mandatory department, and omitting UNIQUE allows multiple employee rows to reference the same department. A scalar employee reference in Department cannot represent an arbitrary employee set.

questions.question: Students may take many Courses, Courses may have many Students, and each student-course pair has one current Grade. Which relational mapping represents this many-to-many relationship without storing a list in a cell?

options.A: One CourseID column in Student, with no association table
options.B: Enrollment(StudentID,CourseID,Grade), with StudentID alone as its primary key
options.C: Enrollment(StudentID,CourseID,Grade), with primary key (StudentID,CourseID) and foreign keys to both entity tables
options.D: One StudentID column in Course, with no association table

questions.explanation: The bridge relation stores one row per association and keeps Grade on that association. The composite primary key prevents duplicate current enrollment pairs without limiting a student or course to only one partner.

questions.question: Dependent is a weak entity owned by Employee. DependentName is unique only within one employee's dependents; the same name may occur for different employees. Which primary key correctly identifies a dependent?

options.D: A constant identifying the Dependent entity type

questions.explanation: The owner key plus the weak entity's partial key provides global identification. EmployeeID alone would permit only one dependent per owner, while DependentName alone would incorrectly prohibit repeated names across owners.

questions.question: An Employee may belong to zero or one Department; a Department may have many Employees. A scalar DepartmentID column is placed in Employee. Which definition represents this optional many-to-one relationship?

options.A: A NOT NULL UNIQUE DepartmentID foreign key
options.B: An unconstrained DepartmentID that may refer to a nonexistent Department
options.C: A nullable UNIQUE DepartmentID foreign key
options.D: A nullable DepartmentID foreign key with no UNIQUE constraint on DepartmentID

questions.explanation: NULL represents no department, and a non-NULL foreign-key value must name an existing department. Not making the column UNIQUE allows many employees to share a department. NOT NULL would remove the optional case.

questions.question: A B+ tree internal node occupies one 4,096-byte page with a 64-byte header. It stores m child pointers of 8 bytes each and m-1 keys of 8 bytes each, with no other storage costs. What is the pair (maximum child pointers, maximum separator keys)?
questions.explanation: The size constraint is 64 + 8m + 8(m-1) <= 4,096, or 16m <= 4,040. Thus m <= 252.5, so the largest integer m is 252 and the separator count is 251.

questions.question: A B+ tree leaf page is 4,096 bytes. It has a 64-byte header plus a separate 8-byte next-leaf pointer. Each entry occupies 8 bytes for its key and 8 bytes for its record identifier. Entries are not compressed and have no other overhead. How many entries fit in one leaf?
questions.explanation: Entry space is 4,096 - 64 - 8 = 4,024 bytes. Each entry needs 16 bytes, so floor(4,024/16) = 251 entries fit. The next-leaf pointer is additional to the header.

questions.question: A B+ tree has height 3, defined as three edges from root to leaf. Every internal node, including the root, can have at most 100 children, and each leaf holds at most 80 record entries. All records occur only at leaves. What is the maximum record count?
questions.explanation: Three internal branching steps can produce 100^3 = 1,000,000 leaves. At 80 records per leaf, the maximum is 80 * 100^3 = 80,000,000 records. Counting only two branching steps would confuse edges with levels.

questions.question: A B+ tree stores exactly 1,000,000 record entries. Each leaf can hold at most 100 entries, and each internal node, including the root, can have at most 100 children. Height is the number of root-to-leaf edges, with a root-only leaf having height 0. What is the minimum possible height, assuming full nodes are allowed?
questions.explanation: A height-h tree can hold at most 100 * 100^h entries. Height 1 holds only 10,000, while height 2 holds 1,000,000. Thus two edges, or three node levels, suffice and are necessary.

questions.question: A B-tree has minimum degree t=3 and height 2 edges. A non-root node has t-1 through 2t-1 keys; an internal node has one more child than keys. The internal root has at least one key and at most 2t-1 keys, and all leaves are at depth 2. Counting keys in every node, what is the pair (minimum keys, maximum keys)?
questions.explanation: The sparsest tree has one root key, two children with two keys each, and six leaves with two keys each: 1 + 4 + 12 = 17. The fullest tree has 1 + 6 + 36 nodes, each with five keys, for 43 * 5 = 215.

questions.question: A clustered B+ tree stores each full record in its leaf and has height 3 edges. For one successful equality lookup, the root page is already cached, but every other page on the search path is uncached. There is no read-ahead and no separate heap fetch. How many disk-page reads are needed?
