questions.question: A server authenticates a user successfully but refuses a requested operation because that user lacks the required role. It chooses to disclose this authorization refusal. Which status fits?

options.D: 401 Unauthorized solely because any refusal is an authentication failure

questions.explanation: 403 expresses that the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it. The stated reason is authorization, not missing or invalid authentication.

questions.module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
questions.question: An origin server encounters an unexpected internal exception while processing an otherwise valid request and cannot complete it. Which general status fits this failure?
questions.explanation: 500 represents an unexpected server condition that prevents fulfillment. More specific gateway and temporary-unavailability conditions are not stated here.

questions.module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
questions.question: Scenario A: a reverse proxy receives an invalid response from its upstream while serving a request. Scenario B: an origin server temporarily cannot serve requests because it is overloaded. Which status pairing is most precise?

options.A: A: 404 Not Found; B: 400 Bad Request
options.B: A: 503 Service Unavailable; B: 502 Bad Gateway
options.D: A: 502 Bad Gateway; B: 503 Service Unavailable

questions.explanation: 502 describes an invalid upstream response received by a gateway. 503 describes temporary inability to serve, such as overload or scheduled maintenance; Retry-After may describe a recovery delay.

questions.module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
questions.question: Which design best satisfies REST constraints concerning stateless interactions, cacheability, and layered systems?

options.A: Each request carries needed interaction context, responses indicate caching rules, and clients need not know every intermediary layer
options.B: Every response must be unconditionally cached forever even when personalized
options.C: Every request depends on private conversational state stored only in the previous server process
options.D: Clients must bypass every intermediary and contact the origin implementation directly

questions.explanation: REST combines self-contained interactions, explicit cache semantics, and a layered architecture. It does not require process-local conversational state, direct-only connections, or indiscriminate caching.

questions.module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
questions.question: In a conventional server-side login-session design, a browser stores an opaque session ID in a cookie. Where is the associated server-side session state normally stored?

options.A: Inside the Cookie header as an automatically embedded complete server memory snapshot
options.B: Necessarily inside localStorage because every cookie is a storage pointer
options.C: In a server-side session store indexed by that identifier
options.D: Necessarily inside the browser's sessionStorage because the word session is used

questions.explanation: A server-side session ID identifies state held by the service, perhaps in a shared database or cache. A login session is not the same concept as the sessionStorage browser API.

questions.module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
questions.question: Assume ordinary first-party pages with storage enabled and no additional partitioning distinctions. Which page shares the localStorage origin of https://example.com/app?
questions.explanation: Web Storage is associated with an origin, whose scheme, host, and effective port must match. A path change keeps the origin; the other choices change one of those components.

questions.module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
questions.question: Browser JavaScript on https://app.example wants to send a cross-origin PUT to https://api.example with Content-Type: application/json. No cached preflight permission exists. What permission-check request does CORS normally require first?

options.B: The PUT must always be sent directly without any preflight
options.C: POST with Access-Control-Allow-Origin set by the client

questions.explanation: PUT is not a CORS-safelisted method, and application/json is not a safelisted Content-Type. An OPTIONS preflight asks whether the target permits the actual method and relevant headers.

questions.module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
questions.question: A browser fetch from https://app.example to https://api.example uses credentials: "include". Cookie policy permits the eligible cookie, the GET reaches the server, and no other blocking policy applies. The response headers are shown. Why can the script not read the response?
questions.code_snippet:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Content-Type: application/json

{"balance": 42}

options.A: All cross-origin GET requests require a POST preflight first
options.B: Credentialed CORS requires a matching explicit allowed origin; wildcard * does not satisfy it
options.C: The request cannot have reached the server because every CORS error prevents network transmission
options.D: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials must be changed from true to false

questions.explanation: With credentials mode include, Access-Control-Allow-Origin cannot be *. A matching explicit origin plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is needed to expose the response; read blocking does not prove the request was unsent.

questions.module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
questions.question: A browser uses ordinary fetch to make a cross-origin POST with credentials: "omit", Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, no custom headers, and a simple string body. No other policy or transport restriction applies. The server accepts the request and changes its data but returns no CORS response headers. Which outcome is correct?

options.A: The POST can be sent and processed, but the browser blocks script access to its response
options.B: The response is always readable because the POST Content-Type is safelisted
options.C: Omitting CORS response headers automatically rolls back the server's data change
options.D: The browser must preflight every POST and never sends this one

questions.explanation: This request does not require preflight under the stated conditions. Missing CORS permission prevents response exposure to the script; it does not undo a request the server has already processed.

questions.module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
questions.question: An API defines two PATCH documents with the exact sequential operations shown. Each resource starts with counter=3. Each document is applied twice to its own resource, without other writes. Considering only the intended counter state, which statement is correct?
questions.code_snippet:
PATCH document A:
    set counter = 5
    increment counter by 1

PATCH document B:
    increment counter by 2

options.A: A is idempotent and ends at 6; B is not idempotent and ends at 7
options.B: Both are idempotent and both end at 6
options.C: A is non-idempotent and ends at 12; B is idempotent and ends at 5
options.D: Both are non-idempotent merely because the HTTP method is PATCH

questions.explanation: A resets to 5 before incrementing, so each complete application ends at 6. B increments the existing state by two each time, producing 3->5->7. PATCH can be designed idempotently but is not generally guaranteed to be.

questions.module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
questions.question: A same-origin page stores token L in localStorage and has eligible login cookie S marked Secure and HttpOnly. An injected same-origin script executes with ordinary page privileges, and no additional policy blocks its requests. Which capability description is accurate?

options.A: It can read L and issue same-origin authenticated requests using S, but cannot directly read S through document.cookie
options.B: It can read S but localStorage is automatically hidden from same-origin JavaScript
options.C: It can read neither L nor S and cannot issue authenticated requests
options.D: It can read both L and S because HttpOnly affects only transport encryption

questions.explanation: localStorage is script-accessible for the origin. HttpOnly hides S from script cookie-reading APIs, but the browser can still attach that eligible cookie to script-initiated requests. Secure restricts its transport to secure channels.

questions.module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
questions.question: No preflight cache entry exists for the proposed cross-origin PUT. Its requested unsafe header names and the server's preflight response are shown. Credentials mode is omit, there are no redirects, and every other policy check passes. What does the browser do next?
questions.code_snippet:
OPTIONS /items/7 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example
Origin: https://app.example
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization, content-type

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PUT
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type

options.A: Treat the OPTIONS 200 as the completed PUT response without sending the update
options.B: Send the PUT because allowing its method automatically allows every header
options.C: Fail the preflight and withhold the PUT because authorization is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Headers
options.D: Send the PUT but silently strip Authorization while retaining the application's intended request

questions.explanation: The preflight must authorize the method and all relevant unsafe request headers. Content-Type alone does not authorize Authorization, so the actual PUT is not sent under these assumptions.

questions.question: What is the arithmetic mean of 2, 4, 6, and 8?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Sum the observations: 2+4+6+8=20. Step 2: Divide by the count 4: mean=20/4=5.

questions.question: What is the median of the ordered observations 2, 3, 7, and 9?
questions.explanation: Step 1: There are four observations, so use the two middle values, 3 and 7. Step 2: Their average is (3+7)/2=5.

questions.question: What is the unique mode of 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 5?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Count frequencies: 2 occurs twice, 3 once, and 5 three times. Step 2: The highest frequency belongs to 5, so it is the unique mode.

questions.question: Treat 1 and 3 as an entire population. What is their population variance?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The population mean is (1+3)/2=2. Step 2: The squared deviations are 1 and 1. Step 3: Divide their sum by N=2: variance=2/2=1.

questions.question: For the sample 2, 4, 6, what is the sample variance using denominator n-1?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The sample mean is 4. Step 2: Squared deviations sum to 4+0+4=8. Step 3: Divide by n-1=2: s^2=8/2=4.

questions.question: A population has variance 9. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of variance. Step 2: sqrt(9)=3; its units match the original observations.

questions.question: A dataset has first quartile Q1=12 and third quartile Q3=19. What is its interquartile range?
questions.explanation: Step 1: IQR is Q3-Q1. Step 2: Subtract 12 from 19 to obtain 7.

questions.question: A distribution has positive finite variance and a strictly positive third central moment. What is the sign of its population moment skewness E[(X-mu)^3]/sigma^3?

options.C: Undefined solely because the third moment is positive

questions.explanation: Step 1: sigma^3 is positive because variance is positive. Step 2: A positive third central moment divided by a positive denominator gives positive moment skewness.

questions.question: Using excess kurtosis = E[(X-mu)^4]/sigma^4 - 3, what is the excess kurtosis when the standardized fourth central moment is 3.8?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The supplied 3.8 is raw standardized kurtosis. Step 2: Subtract the normal-distribution reference 3: excess kurtosis=3.8-3=0.8.

questions.question: If P(A intersect B)=0.12 and P(B)=0.30, what is P(A|B)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: P(A|B)=P(A intersect B)/P(B). Step 2: Since P(B)>0, compute 0.12/0.30=0.4.

questions.question: If P(A)=0.27, what is the probability of the complement of A?
questions.explanation: Step 1: A and its complement partition the sample space. Step 2: P(not A)=1-P(A)=1-0.27=0.73.

questions.question: A discrete random variable X equals 0 with probability 0.25 and 2 with probability 0.75. What is E[X]?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Multiply each value by its probability. Step 2: E[X]=0(0.25)+2(0.75)=1.5.

questions.question: X is Bernoulli with P(X=1)=0.2 and P(X=0)=0.8. What is Var(X)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: E[X]=E[X^2]=0.2 because X is zero or one. Step 2: Var(X)=E[X^2]-E[X]^2=0.2-0.04=0.16.

questions.question: For 1, 2, 3, 4, 100, what ordered pair gives the median followed by the arithmetic mean?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The middle of the five ordered values is 3. Step 2: The total is 110, so the mean is 110/5=22. The large final value affects the mean much more than the median.

questions.question: Team A has 20 scores with mean 70; Team B has 30 scores with mean 80. What is the mean of all 50 scores?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Recover totals: 20(70)=1400 and 30(80)=2400. Step 2: Combine totals and counts: (1400+2400)/(20+30)=3800/50=76.

questions.question: A random observation comes equally likely from two populations. Their means are 2 and 6, and each has population variance 1. What is the variance of the mixture?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The mixture mean is (2+6)/2=4. Step 2: Average within-group variance is 1. Step 3: Variance of group means is ((2-4)^2+(6-4)^2)/2=4. Total variance is 1+4=5.

questions.question: E[X]=4 and Var(X)=5. For Y=3X-2, what are E[Y] and Var(Y)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: E[Y]=3E[X]-2=3(4)-2=10. Step 2: A constant shift does not affect variance, while multiplication by 3 multiplies it by 9. Var(Y)=9(5)=45.

questions.question: What is the sample standard deviation of 1, 2, 3, using denominator n-1 in the sample variance?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Mean=2 and squared deviations sum to 1+0+1=2. Step 2: Sample variance is 2/(3-1)=1. Step 3: Sample standard deviation is sqrt(1)=1.

questions.question: For ordered data 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11, 13, define Q1 and Q3 as the medians of the lower four and upper four observations. What is the IQR?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Lower-half median Q1=(2+4)/2=3. Step 2: Upper-half median Q3=(9+11)/2=10. Step 3: IQR=10-3=7. This explicitly uses the stated median-of-halves convention.

questions.question: X takes values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3 respectively. What is Var(X)?
Independent random variables X and Y have variances 4 and 9. What is Var(X+Y)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Independence implies Cov(X,Y)=0 when second moments exist. Step 2: Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y)=4+9=13.

questions.question: Var(X)=4, Var(Y)=9, and Cov(X,Y)=-2. What is Var(X+Y)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Expand Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y). Step 2: Substitute 4+9+2(-2)=13-4=9; the covariance term cannot be omitted.

questions.question: Factory A supplies 60% of units and has a 2% defect rate. Factory B supplies 40% and has a 5% defect rate. A randomly selected unit is defective. What is the probability it came from B?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Defective-unit probabilities are 0.6(0.02)=0.012 from A and 0.4(0.05)=0.020 from B. Step 2: Total defect probability is 0.032. Step 3: Bayes gives 0.020/0.032=5/8.

questions.question: One percent of transactions are fraudulent. A flagging system flags 90% of fraud and 10% of legitimate transactions. What fraction of flagged transactions are fraudulent?
questions.explanation: Step 1: True-positive mass is 0.01(0.90)=0.009. Step 2: False-positive mass is 0.99(0.10)=0.099. Step 3: Among flags, fraud probability is 0.009/(0.009+0.099)=1/12.

questions.question: Choose one of two boxes with equal probability. Box 1 has two red balls and one blue; Box 2 has one red and two blue. Draw one uniformly selected ball. Given that it is red, what is P(Box 1|red)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Joint red probabilities are (1/2)(2/3)=1/3 from Box 1 and (1/2)(1/3)=1/6 from Box 2. Step 2: Normalize: (1/3)/(1/3+1/6)=2/3.

questions.question: An urn has three red and two blue balls. Two balls are drawn uniformly without replacement. What is the probability both are red?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The first red has probability 3/5. Step 2: After drawing red, two red remain among four balls, so the next red has probability 2/4. Step 3: Multiply to get (3/5)(2/4)=3/10.

questions.question: Two independent fair coins are tossed. You are told only that at least one is heads. What is the conditional probability both are heads?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The equally likely ordered outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT. Step 2: The information excludes TT, leaving three outcomes. Step 3: Only HH has two heads, so the conditional probability is 1/3.

questions.question: P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, and P(A intersect B)=0.2. Which relationship is established?

options.A: A and B are both independent and mutually exclusive
options.B: A and B are mutually exclusive but not independent
options.C: A and B are independent but not mutually exclusive
options.D: A and B are neither independent nor mutually exclusive

questions.explanation: Step 1: P(A)P(B)=0.4(0.5)=0.2 equals the intersection, so the events are independent. Step 2: Their intersection has positive probability, so they are not mutually exclusive.

questions.question: Thirty percent of visitors are in segment A and 70% in segment B. Purchase probabilities are 0.2 in A and 0.1 in B. What is the overall purchase probability?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Weight each conditional purchase probability by its segment share. Step 2: P(purchase)=0.3(0.2)+0.7(0.1)=0.06+0.07=0.13.

questions.question: A game pays 10 units with probability 0.2 and zero otherwise. Entering costs 1 unit regardless of outcome. What is the expected net gain?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Expected gross payout is 10(0.2)+0(0.8)=2. Step 2: Subtract the certain entry cost: expected net gain=2-1=1.

questions.question: E[X]=3 and E[Y]=5, with no independence assumption. What is E[2X-Y]?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Linearity of expectation gives E[2X-Y]=2E[X]-E[Y], regardless of dependence. Step 2: Substitute 2(3)-5=1.

questions.question: Var(X)=4 and Y=2X+3. What is Cov(X,Y)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Cov(X,2X+3)=2Cov(X,X)+Cov(X,3). Step 2: A constant has zero covariance, so the result is 2Var(X)=2(4)=8.

questions.question: A target class has prevalence 0.2. Each of two detectors has sensitivity 0.8 and false-positive probability 0.1. Their outcomes are independent conditional on class membership. Both return positive. What is the posterior target probability?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Conditional independence gives P(++|target)=0.8^2=0.64 and P(++|not target)=0.1^2=0.01. Step 2: Weighted masses are 0.2(0.64)=0.128 and 0.8(0.01)=0.008. Step 3: Normalize: 0.128/0.136=16/17.

questions.question: Ten percent of items belong to a target class. A detector has sensitivity 0.9 and false-positive probability 0.2. Given a negative result, what is the probability the item belongs to the target class?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Negative target mass is 0.1(1-0.9)=0.01. Step 2: Negative non-target mass is 0.9(1-0.2)=0.72. Step 3: The posterior is 0.01/(0.01+0.72)=1/73.

questions.question: The entire population contains values 1, 1, 3, 5. What is its population variance?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Mean=(1+1+3+5)/4=2.5. Step 2: Squared deviations sum to 2.25+2.25+0.25+6.25=11. Step 3: Divide by population size 4: variance=11/4=2.75.

questions.question: X has population moment skewness 0.6 and positive finite variance. What is the moment skewness of Y=7-2X?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Centering gives Y-E[Y]=-2(X-E[X]), so the third central moment is multiplied by -8. Step 2: The standard deviation is multiplied by 2, so its cube is multiplied by 8. Step 3: The standardized ratio changes sign only: -0.6.

questions.question: In a three-door game, the prize is uniformly assigned to one door. You choose a door. A knowledgeable host always opens an unchosen empty door, choosing uniformly if both are empty, and always offers a switch to the remaining unopened door. What is the probability of winning by switching?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Your initial door has the prize with probability 1/3, and an unchosen door has it with probability 2/3. Step 2: The host always removes an empty option. Step 3: Switching wins exactly when the initial choice was wrong, so its win probability is 2/3.

questions.question: Choose uniformly among boxes GG, GS, SS, where G is a gold coin and S a silver coin. Then choose one of the selected box's two coins uniformly and observe gold. What is the probability the other coin in that box is also gold?
questions.explanation: Step 1: There are six equally likely box-and-position choices. Step 2: Three reveal gold: two positions in GG and one in GS. Step 3: Two of those three choices leave another gold coin, giving 2/3.

questions.question: Two campaigns have the segment results shown. Comparing observed conversion fractions only, which statement is correct?
questions.code_snippet:
Campaign | Easy segment conversions/visitors | Hard segment conversions/visitors
A        | 80/100                           | 20/100
B        | 90/120                           | 1/10

options.A: A has a lower rate in each segment but a higher pooled rate
options.B: A has a higher rate in each segment but a lower pooled rate
options.C: Both campaigns have identical pooled rates
options.D: A has a higher rate in each segment and also a higher pooled rate

questions.explanation: Step 1: In the easy segment, A=80/100=0.80 and B=90/120=0.75. Step 2: In the hard segment, A=20/100=0.20 and B=1/10=0.10. Step 3: Pooled A=100/200=0.50, but B=91/130=0.70. Different segment weights reverse the aggregate comparison; this alone is not a causal conclusion.

questions.question: A family has two children whose sexes are independent and equally likely boy or girl. An observer chooses one of the two children uniformly, independently of sex, and reports that the chosen child is a boy. Under this reporting protocol, what is the probability both children are boys?
questions.explanation: Step 1: P(BB)=1/4, and a selected child is certainly a boy under BB. Step 2: P(selected child is boy)=1/2. Step 3: Bayes gives (1/4)/(1/2)=1/2. The random-child protocol differs from merely conditioning on at least one boy.

questions.question: Before ten trials, a latent probability P is chosen as 0.2 or 0.8 with equal probability. Conditional on P, the ten Bernoulli trials are independent with success probability P. If S counts successes, what is Var(S)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: E[P(1-P)]=0.16, so E[Var(S|P)]=10(0.16)=1.6. Step 2: E[P]=0.5 and Var(P)=0.09, so Var(E[S|P])=Var(10P)=100(0.09)=9. Step 3: Total variance is 1.6+9=10.6; unconditional trials are not independent.

questions.question: X is uniform on {-1,0,1} and Y=X^2. Which statement about covariance and independence is correct?

options.A: Cov(X,Y)=1/3, and X and Y are independent
options.B: Cov(X,Y)=0, and X and Y are independent
options.C: Cov(X,Y)=0, but X and Y are dependent
options.D: Cov(X,Y)=2/3, and X and Y are dependent

questions.explanation: Step 1: E[X]=0, E[Y]=2/3, and E[XY]=E[X^3]=0, so covariance is zero. Step 2: P(Y=0|X=0)=1, whereas P(Y=0)=1/3. Thus zero covariance does not imply independence here.

questions.question: X equals 0 with probability 0.9 and each of -sqrt(10), +sqrt(10) with probability 0.05. Using excess kurtosis E[(X-mu)^4]/sigma^4 - 3, what is its excess kurtosis?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Symmetry gives mu=0. Step 2: E[X^2]=0.05(10)+0.05(10)=1, so sigma^4=1. Step 3: E[X^4]=0.05(100)+0.05(100)=10. Step 4: Excess kurtosis=10/1-3=7.

questions.question: Four random variables each have variance 9, and every distinct pair has correlation 1/3. What is the variance of their arithmetic mean?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Each pair has covariance (1/3)(3)(3)=3. Step 2: The sum variance is 4(9)+2(6 pairs)(3)=72. Step 3: Dividing the sum by 4 divides its variance by 16: Var(mean)=72/16=4.5.

questions.question: Two independent fair six-sided dice are rolled. Given that the maximum of the two results is exactly 4, what is the conditional expected sum?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The seven qualifying ordered pairs are (4,1),(4,2),(4,3),(4,4),(1,4),(2,4),(3,4). Step 2: Their sums are 5,6,7,8,5,6,7, totaling 44. Step 3: All seven are equally likely, so the conditional expected sum is 44/7.

questions.question: What are the mean and standard deviation of a standard normal random variable?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Standardization subtracts the population mean, producing mean zero. Step 2: Dividing by the population standard deviation gives variance one and therefore standard deviation one.

questions.question: An observation is 130 from a normal population with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. What is its z-score?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Subtract the mean: 130-100=30. Step 2: Divide by the standard deviation: z=30/15=2.

questions.question: Using the approximate 68-95-99.7 empirical rule for a normal population, what percentage lies within one population standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The interval is mu-sigma to mu+sigma. Step 2: The empirical rule allocates approximately 68% to this interval; 95% and 99.7% correspond to two and three standard deviations.

questions.question: Using the approximate 68-95-99.7 rule, what percentage of a normal population lies outside the interval mu +/- 2 sigma?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Approximately 95% lies inside the two-standard-deviation interval. Step 2: Its complement is 100%-95%=5%, split approximately equally between the two tails.

questions.question: A study tests whether a population mean differs from 100 in either direction. Which hypotheses express that two-sided question?

options.A: H0: sample mean=100; H1: sample mean!=100

questions.explanation: Step 1: Hypotheses concern the population parameter mu, not the random sample statistic. Step 2: The equality is the null, and differences in either direction give the alternative mu!=100.

questions.question: Which event is a Type I error in hypothesis testing?

options.A: Failing to reject H0 when H0 is false
options.B: Rejecting H0 when H0 is false
options.C: Failing to reject H0 when H0 is true
options.D: Rejecting H0 when H0 is true

questions.explanation: Step 1: Condition on a true null hypothesis. Step 2: An erroneous rejection is a Type I error; its probability is controlled by the test's significance level alpha.

questions.question: Which event is a Type II error at a specified alternative?

options.A: Rejecting H0 when that alternative is true
options.B: Rejecting H0 when H0 is true
options.C: Failing to reject H0 when that alternative is true
options.D: Obtaining a p-value smaller than alpha under any circumstance

questions.explanation: Step 1: Consider a specified false-null parameter value. Step 2: Failing to reject at that value is a Type II error, with probability beta. Correct rejection has probability 1-beta.

questions.question: A test has Type II error probability beta=0.20 at a specified alternative. What is its power there?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Power is the probability of correctly rejecting under the specified alternative. Step 2: Power=1-beta=1-0.20=0.80.

questions.question: For a prespecified test statistic and extremeness rule, which statement correctly defines a p-value?

options.A: Under H0, the probability of a statistic at least as extreme as the observed one
options.B: The probability that the next replication will reject H0
options.C: The probability that the observed numerical statistic occurs exactly in any continuous model
options.D: The probability that H0 is true after observing the sample

questions.explanation: Step 1: Use the statistic's sampling distribution assuming H0 and the test assumptions. Step 2: Sum the probability of outcomes at least as extreme under the prespecified direction or two-sided rule. This is not a posterior probability of H0.

questions.question: A valid prespecified test reports p=0.03. At alpha=0.05, what is the decision?

options.B: Conclude the effect must be practically large
options.C: Fail to reject H0 because p must be below 0.01

questions.explanation: Step 1: Compare p to alpha: 0.03<0.05. Step 2: Reject H0 at the 5% significance level. The decision alone establishes neither practical importance nor a posterior null probability.

questions.question: An independent random sample comes from a normal population whose population standard deviation sigma is known. Which statistic gives an exact one-sample test of H0: mu=mu0?

options.A: A chi-square independence statistic on the original numerical values
options.B: Z=(sample mean-mu0)/(sigma/sqrt(n)), compared with standard normal
options.C: An ANOVA statistic requiring at least three sample means
options.D: T=(sample mean-mu0)/(sigma/sqrt(n)), compared only with chi-square

questions.explanation: Step 1: Normal sampling implies the sample mean is normal with standard error sigma/sqrt(n). Step 2: Under H0, subtracting mu0 and dividing by that known standard error gives an exact standard normal statistic.

questions.question: Ten independent observations come from a normal population with unknown variance. A one-sample mean test uses the sample standard deviation s. Which reference distribution is exact under H0?

options.A: Standard normal solely because n is positive
options.B: Student t with 10 degrees of freedom
options.D: Student t with 9 degrees of freedom

questions.explanation: Step 1: Estimating sigma with s makes (sample mean-mu0)/(s/sqrt(n)) a t statistic under normal sampling. Step 2: The degrees of freedom are n-1=10-1=9.

questions.question: Independent observations have population standard deviation 12. For a sample size of 36, what is the standard error of the sample mean?
questions.explanation: Step 1: SE(sample mean)=sigma/sqrt(n). Step 2: sqrt(36)=6, so SE=12/6=2.

questions.question: For an independent normal sample, sample mean=103, H0 mean=100, known sigma=12, and n=36. What is the z statistic?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The standard error is 12/sqrt(36)=2. Step 2: The difference is 103-100=3. Step 3: z=3/2=1.5.

questions.question: For an independent normal sample with n=16, sample mean=52, sample standard deviation s=4, and H0 mean=50, what is the one-sample t statistic?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Estimated standard error is 4/sqrt(16)=1. Step 2: Divide the mean difference by this error: t=(52-50)/1=2; its null reference has 15 degrees of freedom.

questions.question: The same 20 employees are measured before and after training. Employees are independent, and the within-person differences are approximately normal with unknown variance. Which test directly targets the mean change?

options.A: A chi-square test of categorical independence
options.B: A one-sample z-test assuming the difference variance is known
options.C: A paired t-test on the 20 differences
options.D: An independent-samples pooled t-test treating all 40 measurements as unrelated

questions.explanation: Step 1: Subtract before from after for each employee, giving 20 paired differences. Step 2: Test mean difference zero using t=mean(d)/(s_d/sqrt(20)) with 19 degrees of freedom. Pairing retains the within-person dependence.

questions.question: Two independent normal populations have unknown variances, and equal population variances cannot be assumed. Which listed mean-comparison test avoids pooling those variances?

options.A: Paired t-test on arbitrarily matched subjects
options.C: Chi-square independence test on the numerical means

questions.explanation: Step 1: The samples are independent, so this is not a paired design. Step 2: Welch uses SE=sqrt(s1^2/n1+s2^2/n2) without assuming equal variances, with an approximate t reference.

questions.question: A random sample is cross-tabulated by region and preferred product category. Observations are independent and all expected cell counts are sufficiently large. Which test addresses association between these categorical variables?

options.A: A one-way ANOVA comparing category labels as arbitrary numbers
options.C: A paired t-test on category names
options.D: A one-sample z-test for a numerical population mean

questions.explanation: Step 1: Both measurements are categorical and produce a contingency table. Step 2: Under independence, expected counts are row total times column total divided by N. Step 3: Compare sum((O-E)^2/E) with the appropriate chi-square reference.

questions.question: Three independent groups have normal errors with a common population variance. A one-way ANOVA tests equality of their means. What is its alternative hypothesis?

options.A: All population variances must be different
options.B: Every pair of group means must differ
options.C: At least one group mean differs

questions.explanation: Step 1: H0 is mu1=mu2=mu3. Step 2: Its complement is that the means are not all equal, so at least one differs. A significant omnibus F-test does not identify every differing pair.

questions.question: In a contingency table with total N=100, a row total is 40 and a column total is 30. What is their intersection cell's expected count under independence?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Under independence, expected count=(row total)(column total)/N. Step 2: Compute 40(30)/100=12.

questions.question: A Pearson chi-square table cell has observed count 18 and expected count 12. What is this cell's contribution to the statistic?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Compute the residual 18-12=6. Step 2: Square it and divide by expected count: (18-12)^2/12=36/12=3.

questions.question: For a standard Pearson independence test on a 3-by-4 contingency table without structural-zero complications, what are the degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The degrees of freedom are (rows-1)(columns-1). Step 2: Substitute (3-1)(4-1)=2(3)=6.

questions.question: A one-way ANOVA has four groups and 20 observations in total. What are its between-group and within-group degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Between-group df=k-1=4-1=3. Step 2: Within-group df=N-k=20-4=16. Their sum 19 equals the total df=N-1.

questions.question: An ANOVA reports between-group mean square 12 and within-group mean square 3. What is the F statistic?
questions.explanation: Step 1: F is MS_between/MS_within. Step 2: Compute 12/3=4. The reference F distribution uses the corresponding numerator and denominator degrees of freedom.

questions.question: Let Z be standard normal, with Phi(1)=0.8413 and Phi(-1)=0.1587. What is P(-1<Z<1), using these table values?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Subtract the lower cumulative probability from the upper one. Step 2: P(-1<Z<1)=0.8413-0.1587=0.6826. Continuity makes endpoint inclusion immaterial.

questions.question: For standard normal Z, Phi(1.96)=0.9750. What is P(Z>1.96)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The cumulative probability includes values at or below 1.96. Step 2: The upper tail is its complement, 1-0.9750=0.0250.

questions.question: A prespecified two-sided z-test observes z=2.00. Given Phi(2.00)=0.97725, what is its p-value?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The upper-tail probability is 1-0.97725=0.02275. Step 2: Symmetry gives the same lower-tail extremeness probability. Step 3: Two-sided p=2(0.02275)=0.0455.

questions.question: A prespecified upper-tailed z-test has H1: mu>mu0 but observes z=-1.50. Given Phi(-1.50)=0.0668, what is its p-value?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The upper-tailed alternative uses P(Z>=observed z), even if the observed statistic is negative. Step 2: p=1-Phi(-1.50)=1-0.0668=0.9332; switching tails after seeing the data is invalid.

questions.question: A valid test gives p=0.20 at alpha=0.05. Which conclusion is warranted?

options.B: H0 is proven true with probability 0.80
options.C: The data do not provide enough evidence to reject H0 at this level
options.D: The population effect is exactly zero

questions.explanation: Step 1: Since 0.20>0.05, fail to reject H0. Step 2: This is a decision about evidence under a test, not a proof of equality or a computed posterior probability; low power may also produce non-rejection.

questions.question: Independent, identically distributed observations have finite mean and positive finite variance but a skewed population distribution. What does the classical CLT say as n grows?

options.A: The sample variance must become zero
options.B: Every sample of size at least 30 is exactly normal
options.C: The population itself becomes normal as more data are collected
options.D: The standardized sample mean converges in distribution to standard normal

questions.explanation: Step 1: Standardize the mean as sqrt(n)(sample mean-mu)/sigma. Step 2: Under the stated iid finite-variance assumptions, its limiting distribution is N(0,1). This concerns the sampling distribution, not a change in the population shape.

questions.question: For iid observations with fixed finite population variance, how must sample size change to halve the standard error of the sample mean?
questions.explanation: Step 1: SE=sigma/sqrt(n). Step 2: Require sigma/sqrt(n_new)=(1/2)sigma/sqrt(n_old). Step 3: Thus sqrt(n_new)=2sqrt(n_old), giving n_new=4n_old.

questions.question: The same valid test result p=0.03 is assessed first at alpha=0.05 and then at alpha=0.01. How do the decisions change?

options.A: Reject at 0.05; fail to reject at 0.01
options.B: Fail to reject at 0.05; reject at 0.01
options.C: Fail to reject at both levels

questions.explanation: Step 1: At alpha=0.05, 0.03<0.05, so reject. Step 2: At alpha=0.01, 0.03>0.01, so fail to reject. The p-value itself does not change when the reporting threshold changes.

questions.question: X1,...,Xn are iid standard Cauchy random variables. Which statement correctly diagnoses an attempt to apply the classical iid finite-variance CLT to their arithmetic mean?

options.A: Its finite-mean/finite-variance requirements fail; this mean does not gain a normal limit through that theorem
options.B: The sample mean has variance exactly 1/n
options.C: The theorem gives an exact normal mean whenever n>=30
options.D: Finite variance is unnecessary for the classical finite-variance theorem

questions.explanation: Step 1: A standard Cauchy distribution has no finite population mean or variance. Step 2: The cited CLT therefore does not apply. Step 3: In fact, the arithmetic mean remains standard Cauchy for every n, so conventional sigma/sqrt(n) reasoning is unavailable.

questions.question: One hundred jointly Gaussian observations are arranged in ten independent clusters of size ten. Each observation has standard deviation 10; each distinct within-cluster pair has correlation 0.2. What is the standard deviation of the overall sample mean?
questions.explanation: Step 1: A within-cluster covariance is 0.2(10)(10)=20. Step 2: Each cluster sum has variance 10(100)+2(45)(20)=2800. Step 3: Ten independent sums give variance 28000 for the total. Step 4: Divide by 100^2 for the mean: Var=2.8, so SE=sqrt(2.8).

questions.question: Two independent studies test the same true null, each with exact Type I error probability 0.05. A combined reporting rule declares a finding if either study rejects. What is the Type I error probability of that rule?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Under the true null, each study does not reject with probability 0.95. Step 2: Independence gives probability neither rejects=0.95^2=0.9025. Step 3: Probability at least one rejects=1-0.9025=0.0975.

questions.question: Across a population of studies, H0 is true in 90% and a specified alternative in 10%. Each test has false-rejection probability 0.05 under H0 and power 0.80 under that alternative. A randomly chosen study rejects. Under this model, what is P(H0 true|reject)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: True-null rejection mass is 0.90(0.05)=0.045. Step 2: Alternative rejection mass is 0.10(0.80)=0.080. Step 3: Bayes gives 0.045/(0.045+0.080)=0.36=9/25. A 5% test size is not a 5% posterior null probability.

questions.question: Three independent normal groups have a common variance, each has n=5, their sample means are 2,4,6, and the total within-group sum of squares is 24. What is the one-way ANOVA F statistic?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The equal-sized grand mean is 4. Step 2: Between SS=5[(2-4)^2+(4-4)^2+(6-4)^2]=40, so between MS=40/2=20. Step 3: Within df=15-3=12 and within MS=24/12=2. Step 4: F=20/2=10.

questions.question: A 2-by-2 independence table has counts [[30,10],[10,50]]. Use Pearson chi-square without continuity correction. At alpha=0.05 the df=1 critical value is 3.841. Which statistic, rounded to four decimals, and decision are correct?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Row and column totals are both 40,60 with N=100, so expected counts are [[16,24],[24,36]]. Step 2: The squared residual is 196 in every cell. Step 3: Chi-square=196/16+196/24+196/24+196/36=34.0278. Step 4: This exceeds 3.841, so reject independence.

questions.question: An upper-tailed z-test of H0: mu=50 uses n=100, known sigma=10, and rejects for z>1.645. At the specific alternative mu=52, take Phi(-0.355)=0.3613. What are beta and power?
questions.explanation: Step 1: SE=10/sqrt(100)=1. Step 2: Rejection requires sample mean>50+1.645(1)=51.645. Step 3: Under mu=52, the non-rejection cutoff standardizes to (51.645-52)/1=-0.355. Step 4: beta=0.3613 and power=1-0.3613=0.6387.

questions.question: Xi are iid Bernoulli(0.001), and n=100. Does the fact that these variables have finite variance guarantee a good normal approximation for their sample mean at this n?

options.A: No; np=0.1 and P(all zeros)=0.999^100 is about 0.905, so the finite-sample distribution is highly asymmetric
options.B: Yes; n>=30 makes every iid sample mean exactly normal
options.C: No; Bernoulli variables have infinite variance
options.D: Yes; bounded variables always have a symmetric mean distribution for every n

questions.explanation: Step 1: The CLT is an asymptotic statement, not a universal n>=30 guarantee. Step 2: Here the expected success count is np=0.1. Step 3: The probability of zero successes is 0.999^100 approximately 0.9048, leaving a large point mass at zero. Finite variance alone does not ensure a useful normal approximation at n=100.

questions.question: What objective does ordinary least squares linear regression minimize over its coefficients?
questions.explanation: Step 1: For observation i, residual r_i=y_i-x_i^T beta. Step 2: OLS chooses beta to minimize sum_i r_i^2. Absolute residuals define a different optimization problem.

questions.question: In y=X beta+epsilon with full-column-rank fixed X, which error-mean assumption yields conditional unbiasedness of OLS?

options.B: Every predictor must have population mean zero
options.D: Every observed residual must be zero

questions.explanation: Step 1: beta_hat=beta+(X^T X)^(-1)X^T epsilon. Step 2: Taking the conditional expectation gives beta plus a term involving E[epsilon|X]. Step 3: If that conditional mean is zero, E[beta_hat|X]=beta.

questions.question: What does homoscedasticity mean in a linear regression error model?

options.A: The fitted response is constant for all predictor values
options.B: The predictor variables are mutually independent
options.C: The conditional error variance is constant across observations
options.D: All regression coefficients have the same value

questions.explanation: Step 1: Write Var(epsilon_i|X)=sigma_i^2. Step 2: Homoscedasticity imposes sigma_i^2=sigma^2 for each i. It concerns error variance, not equality of coefficients or fitted values.

questions.question: A predictor has auxiliary regression R_j^2=0.8 when regressed on all the other predictors with an intercept. What is VIF_j=1/(1-R_j^2)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Unexplained proportion is 1-0.8=0.2. Step 2: VIF=1/0.2=5, describing variance inflation under the usual OLS comparison.

questions.question: In binary logistic regression, what probability does the sigmoid give at linear score z=0?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Sigmoid(z)=1/(1+exp(-z)). Step 2: At zero, exp(0)=1, so p=1/(1+1)=0.5.

questions.question: Which quantity is modeled as a linear predictor in ordinary binary logistic regression?

options.C: The population variance of every input feature

questions.explanation: Step 1: Odds are p/(1-p). Step 2: Their natural logarithm, the log-odds or logit, equals beta0+beta^T x. Solving for p gives the sigmoid.

questions.question: For every finite real linear score z, what is the range of the mathematical sigmoid 1/(1+exp(-z))?
questions.explanation: Step 1: exp(-z)>0 for finite z. Step 2: The denominator is strictly greater than one, so the result is positive and strictly less than one. Numerical floating-point saturation is not the mathematical function's range.

questions.question: What is the base-2 class entropy of a decision-tree node containing only one class?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The class probabilities are 1 for the present class and 0 for the others. Step 2: Using 0 log2(0)=0 by continuity, entropy=-1 log2(1)=0.

questions.question: A binary classification node has class probabilities 0.5 and 0.5. What is its Gini impurity 1-sum_k p_k^2?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Sum the squared probabilities: 0.5^2+0.5^2=0.5. Step 2: Gini=1-0.5=0.5.

questions.question: Which description identifies bootstrap aggregating, or bagging?

options.A: Fit base learners to bootstrap resamples and aggregate their predictions
options.B: Fit each learner sequentially to the preceding learner's loss gradient by definition
options.C: Replace all predictions with the training-label mean regardless of learner output
options.D: Fit one tree only to observations discarded by every resample

questions.explanation: Step 1: Draw training resamples with replacement. Step 2: Fit base learners to those resamples. Step 3: Aggregate, for example by averaging in regression; fitting need not be sequentially dependent as in boosting.

questions.question: In a typical random forest, why sample a subset of candidate features at each split?

options.A: To make every bootstrap sample contain all observations exactly once
options.B: To guarantee every tree uses exactly the same feature at every depth
options.C: To convert all classification targets into continuous values
options.D: To reduce correlation among trees compared with repeatedly choosing from all features

questions.explanation: Step 1: Strong features can otherwise dominate many trees' splits. Step 2: Random feature subsets diversify those choices. Step 3: Reducing tree correlation can make averaging more effective at reducing variance; it is not a guarantee of independence.

questions.question: For one tree trained on a bootstrap sample, what are that tree's out-of-bag observations?

options.A: The complete test set used to tune all tree parameters
options.B: Only observations that the tree misclassifies
options.C: Training observations not selected into that tree's bootstrap sample
options.D: All observations selected twice or more into the sample

questions.explanation: Step 1: A bootstrap sample draws indices with replacement. Step 2: Original training observations whose indices are never drawn are out of bag for that particular tree. Their labels do not train that tree.

questions.question: Fit y=b0+b1*x by OLS to (x,y)=(0,1),(1,3),(2,5). What are b0 and b1?
questions.explanation: Step 1: x_bar=1 and y_bar=3. Step 2: b1=sum((x-x_bar)(y-y_bar))/sum((x-x_bar)^2)=4/2=2. Step 3: b0=y_bar-b1*x_bar=3-2=1; all residuals are zero.

questions.question: For an unconstrained OLS fit with an intercept, evaluated on its fitting data in exact arithmetic, what is the sum of residuals?

options.B: The sum of the response values

questions.explanation: Step 1: Differentiate RSS=sum(y_i-b0-x_i^T b)^2 with respect to b0. Step 2: At an OLS optimum, -2 sum(r_i)=0. Step 3: Therefore the residual sum is zero, assuming an unconstrained intercept.

questions.question: A full-rank fixed-design linear model has E[epsilon|X]=0 and constant finite error variance, but its errors are not normal. Which statement about OLS is correct?

options.A: OLS cannot be calculated unless the observed response is normal
options.B: Every finite-sample t-test is automatically exact without further assumptions
options.C: OLS must be biased solely because errors are non-normal
options.D: OLS remains conditionally unbiased; normal errors are not required for that property

questions.explanation: Step 1: Conditional unbiasedness follows from E[beta_hat|X]=beta+(X^T X)^(-1)X^T E[epsilon|X]. Step 2: The final term is zero without a normality assumption. Exact finite-sample distributional inference is a separate issue.

questions.question: A model has exactly two nonconstant predictors and an intercept. Their sample correlation is 0.9. What is either predictor's VIF, rounded to four decimals?
questions.explanation: Step 1: In the auxiliary regression on one other predictor with an intercept, R^2=r^2=0.81. Step 2: VIF=1/(1-0.81)=1/0.19=5.2632.

questions.question: Under the standard homoscedastic OLS variance formula, a predictor's VIF is 9. Relative to an orthogonal-predictor comparison with the same error variance and predictor sum of squares, by what factor is its coefficient standard error inflated?
questions.explanation: Step 1: VIF multiplies the coefficient variance, here by 9. Step 2: Standard error is the square root of variance, so its inflation factor is sqrt(9)=3.

questions.question: A logistic regression observation has linear score z=ln(3). What is its predicted positive-class probability?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Odds=exp(z)=3. Step 2: Solve p/(1-p)=3, giving p=3/4=0.75.

questions.question: A binary logistic model has coefficient ln(2) for x. Holding other inputs fixed, what is the effect of increasing x by one unit?

options.B: Add exactly 0.5 to the modeled probability
options.C: Multiply the modeled probability by 2 for every starting probability

questions.explanation: Step 1: A one-unit increase adds ln(2) to log-odds. Step 2: Exponentiating multiplies odds by exp(ln(2))=2. The corresponding probability change depends on the starting odds.

questions.question: A logistic model is logit(p)=ln(3)+x*ln(2). At x=2, what is p?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The score is ln(3)+2ln(2)=ln(12). Step 2: Odds=12. Step 3: Convert odds to probability: p=12/(1+12)=12/13.

questions.question: A logistic classifier uses logit(p)=-ln(3)+x*ln(3) and predicts positive when p>=0.75. For real x, which boundary exactly describes a positive prediction?
questions.explanation: Step 1: p>=0.75 is equivalent to logit(p)>=ln(3). Step 2: -ln(3)+x ln(3)>=ln(3). Step 3: Divide by positive ln(3) to obtain x>=2, including equality.

questions.question: A binary decision-tree node contains three positives and one negative. What is its base-2 entropy, rounded to four decimals?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Class proportions are 3/4 and 1/4. Step 2: H=-(3/4)log2(3/4)-(1/4)log2(1/4)=0.811278... Step 3: Round to 0.8113; 0.375 is the Gini impurity, not entropy.

questions.question: A parent has five positives and five negatives. A split makes a left child of four positives and two negatives and a right child of one positive and three negatives. What is the sample-weighted Gini impurity reduction?

A parent node has four positives and four negatives. Two equal-size children have class counts (3 positive,1 negative) and (1 positive,3 negative). What is base-2 information gain, rounded to four decimals?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Parent entropy is 1 bit. Step 2: Each child has entropy -0.75log2(0.75)-0.25log2(0.25)=0.811278... Step 3: Equal weights leave the same child average, so gain=1-0.811278...=0.1887.

questions.question: A parent has four positives and four negatives. Split A forms two pure children of size four; split B forms children with counts (3,1) and (1,3). Which split has larger sample-weighted Gini reduction, and what is that reduction?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Parent Gini is 0.5. Step 2: Split A has zero child impurity, so its gain is 0.5. Step 3: Split B has child impurity 1-(3/4)^2-(1/4)^2=0.375, so its gain is 0.125. A is larger.

questions.question: A regression-tree leaf predicts one constant c for targets 1,2,6 and minimizes sum_i(y_i-c)^2. What prediction minimizes that loss?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Differentiate the loss: -2 sum_i(y_i-c)=0. Step 2: Solve 3c=1+2+6=9, giving c=3. The second derivative is 6>0, so this is the minimum.

questions.question: A bootstrap sample draws four times independently with replacement from four training observations. What is the probability a particular observation is out of bag?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Each draw misses that observation with probability 3/4. Step 2: All four draws must miss it, giving (3/4)^4=81/256. This is an exact finite-sample probability, not the large-n approximation exp(-1).

questions.question: For training observation i, three trees predict positive-class probabilities 0.2,0.9,0.6. Tree 1 trained on a bootstrap containing i, while trees 2 and 3 did not. If OOB prediction is the mean of eligible probabilities, what is i's OOB probability?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Exclude tree 1 because i trained that tree. Step 2: Average the two out-of-bag predictions: (0.9+0.6)/2=0.75. Using all three would leak i into its own OOB prediction.

questions.question: Gradient boosting uses per-observation loss (1/2)(y-F)^2. For targets [3,5] and current predictions [2,2], what are the negative gradients with respect to the predictions?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The prediction derivative is F-y. Step 2: Negate it to obtain y-F. Step 3: Compute [3-2,5-2]=[1,3]; these are the pseudo-residual targets for squared-error boosting.

questions.question: A gradient-boosted model updates F_new=F_old+eta*h. At one observation F_old=2, tree output h=5, and eta=0.1. What is F_new?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Shrink the new tree contribution: eta*h=0.1(5)=0.5. Step 2: Add it to the existing model: F_new=2+0.5=2.5.

questions.question: For loss (1/2)(y-F)^2, a boosting step fits a constant leaf to pseudo-residuals from targets [0,4] and current predictions [1,1]. With learning rate 1, what are the two updated predictions?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Pseudo-residuals are [-1,3]. Step 2: A squared-loss constant leaf fits their mean (-1+3)/2=1. Step 3: Add this leaf output to each old prediction, yielding [2,2]; the leaf cannot fit the two residuals separately.

questions.question: For one positive observation y=1, a classifier predicts p=0.8. What is binary negative log-likelihood loss using natural logarithms, rounded to four decimals?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Binary loss is -[y ln(p)+(1-y)ln(1-p)]. Step 2: With y=1, only -ln(0.8) remains. Step 3: -ln(0.8)=0.223143..., rounded to 0.2231.

questions.question: Centered predictors X1 and X2 are independent with variance 1, and X3=X1+X2. A regression uses all three columns. Which multicollinearity diagnosis is correct?

options.A: The dependence disappears automatically after centering the columns
options.B: The design is rank-deficient and VIF for X3 is unbounded, even though no predictor pair has absolute correlation 1
options.C: The design is full rank because no predictor pair has absolute correlation 1
options.D: VIF for X3 is 1 because X1 and X2 are independent

questions.explanation: Step 1: The exact relation X3-X1-X2=0 makes the three-column design rank-deficient. Step 2: Regressing X3 on X1,X2 gives R^2=1, so 1/(1-R^2) diverges. Step 3: Corr(X1,X3)=Corr(X2,X3)=1/sqrt(2), showing pairwise checks can miss a multivariate dependence.

questions.question: Three centered, standardized predictors have correlation matrix [[1,0.6,0.6],[0.6,1,0],[0.6,0,1]]. What is the first predictor's VIF when an intercept is included?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Predictors 2 and 3 are uncorrelated with one another, so the first predictor's auxiliary R^2 is 0.6^2+0.6^2=0.72. Step 2: VIF=1/(1-0.72)=1/0.28=25/7. Using just one pairwise correlation would understate the result.

questions.question: An unpenalized regression without an intercept has two identical nonzero predictor columns x and x, with response y=3x exactly. Which description of its OLS minimizers is correct?

options.A: No fitted values can exist because the coefficient solution is nonunique
options.C: Every coefficient pair is optimal regardless of its sum
options.D: Every pair satisfying beta1+beta2=3 is optimal; coefficients are nonunique but fitted values are unique

questions.explanation: Step 1: Predictions equal (beta1+beta2)x. Step 2: RSS=(3-beta1-beta2)^2 sum_i x_i^2, and the sum of squares is positive. Step 3: Minimum zero occurs for every pair with sum 3; all such pairs predict 3x.

questions.question: For one observation with x=2,y=1, let z=w*x, p=sigmoid(z), and L=-[y ln(p)+(1-y)ln(1-p)]. At w=0, what are dL/dw and d^2L/dw^2?
questions.explanation: Step 1: At w=0, z=0 and p=0.5. Step 2: Gradient is (p-y)x=(0.5-1)(2)=-1. Step 3: Hessian is p(1-p)x^2=0.5(0.5)(4)=1.

questions.question: An unregularized logistic regression has no intercept and data (x,y)=(-1,0),(1,1). Its coefficient is w. Which statement about the maximum-likelihood estimate is correct?

options.A: No finite minimizer exists; total negative log-likelihood decreases toward zero as w tends to positive infinity
options.B: The unique finite optimum is w=1
options.C: The unique finite optimum is w=0
options.D: The loss decreases toward zero only as w tends to negative infinity

questions.explanation: Step 1: For both observations, the negative log-likelihood is ln(1+exp(-w)). Step 2: Total loss is 2ln(1+exp(-w)), with derivative -2/(1+exp(w))<0 for every finite w. Step 3: Loss approaches zero as w grows without bound, so complete separation prevents a finite unregularized optimum.

questions.question: Ten regression-tree prediction errors at a fixed input each have variance 4, and each distinct pair has correlation 0.25. Their equally weighted average is used. What are its variance and the limiting variance as the number of such equally correlated trees tends to infinity?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Pair covariance is 0.25(4)=1. Step 2: Average variance is [10(4)+2(45)(1)]/100=1.3. Step 3: For T trees it is 4[0.25+0.75/T], which approaches 1, so correlation creates a nonzero averaging floor.

questions.question: For one fixed XGBoost leaf, the second-order objective contribution, excluding constants, is Q(w)=G*w+(1/2)(H+lambda)*w^2. With G=-6,H=2,lambda=1 and no L1 penalty or leaf-count charge, what are the optimal leaf weight and objective reduction Q(0)-Q(w*)?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Differentiate Q: Q'(w)=G+(H+lambda)w=-6+3w. Step 2: Set it to zero, giving w*=2; curvature 3>0 ensures a minimum. Step 3: Q(2)=-12+6=-6 and Q(0)=0, so the reduction is 6.

questions.question: For an XGBoost candidate split, use Gain=(1/2)[G_L^2/(H_L+lambda)+G_R^2/(H_R+lambda)-(G_L+G_R)^2/(H_L+H_R+lambda)]-gamma. Given G_L=-4,H_L=2,G_R=2,H_R=2,lambda=0,gamma=1, what is Gain?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Left and right terms are 16/2=8 and 4/2=2. Step 2: The parent term is (-4+2)^2/(2+2)=4/4=1. Step 3: Gain=(1/2)(8+2-1)-1=4.5-1=3.5. The positive result favors this split under the stated objective.

questions.question: For binary classification with at least one predicted positive, which formula defines positive-class precision?
questions.explanation: Step 1: There are TP+FP predicted positives. Step 2: TP of them are truly positive. Step 3: Precision is the fraction TP/(TP+FP); the denominator assumption avoids division by zero.

questions.question: For binary classification with at least one actual positive, which formula defines positive-class recall?
questions.explanation: Step 1: There are TP+FN actual positives. Step 2: TP are correctly retrieved. Step 3: Recall, also called sensitivity or true-positive rate, is TP/(TP+FN).

questions.question: For binary classification with at least one actual negative, which formula defines specificity?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Actual negatives total TN+FP. Step 2: Correctly rejected negatives total TN. Step 3: Specificity, or true-negative rate, is TN/(TN+FP).

questions.question: A classifier has TP=45,TN=45,FP=5,FN=5. What is its accuracy?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Total cases=45+45+5+5=100. Step 2: Correct cases=TP+TN=90. Step 3: Accuracy=90/100=0.9.

questions.question: When precision P and recall R are positive, which expression defines their F1 score?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The harmonic mean is 2/(1/P+1/R). Step 2: Multiplying numerator and denominator by PR yields 2PR/(P+R). It is not the arithmetic mean.

questions.question: For the standard binary ROC curve, what are the horizontal and vertical axes?

options.A: Horizontal: false-positive rate; vertical: true-positive rate
options.C: Horizontal: true-negative rate; vertical: false-negative rate

questions.explanation: Step 1: At each threshold compute FPR=FP/(FP+TN) and TPR=TP/(TP+FN). Step 2: Plot FPR horizontally and TPR vertically as the threshold varies.

questions.question: Positive and negative cases receive identically distributed continuous scores, independently of their labels. What is the population ROC-AUC?

options.A: The classification accuracy at threshold 0.5 for every prevalence

questions.explanation: Step 1: Identical continuous score distributions give no ties and equal probabilities that either class scores higher. Step 2: P(score_positive>score_negative)=1/2, which is the ranking interpretation of ROC-AUC. This does not fix accuracy at a selected threshold.

questions.question: Which penalty is the conventional squared L2 penalty used in ridge regression?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The squared L2 norm is ||beta||_2^2=sum_j beta_j^2. Step 2: Multiplying by nonnegative lambda penalizes large coefficients smoothly. Intercept treatment must be specified separately in an implementation.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the feature-selection behavior of an L1 penalty in lasso?

options.A: It can set some fitted coefficients exactly to zero
options.B: It guarantees every fitted coefficient is nonzero
options.C: It guarantees exactly one selected feature for every dataset
options.D: It never changes the unpenalized coefficient estimates

questions.explanation: Step 1: The absolute-value penalty has a corner at zero. Step 2: Its subgradient can balance a range of loss gradients at a zero coefficient. Step 3: Exact zeros are possible, although their number and identity depend on the data and penalty.

questions.question: A confusion matrix has TP=40,FP=10,FN=20,TN=130. What are positive-class precision and recall?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Precision=40/(40+10)=40/50=4/5. Step 2: Recall=40/(40+20)=40/60=2/3. True negatives do not enter either denominator.

questions.question: A target population has positive prevalence 0.1. A classifier has recall 0.8 and specificity 0.9 in that population. What is its positive-class precision?
questions.explanation: Step 1: True-positive population mass is 0.1(0.8)=0.08. Step 2: False-positive mass is 0.9(1-0.9)=0.09. Step 3: Precision=0.08/(0.08+0.09)=8/17; it depends on prevalence as well as recall and specificity.

questions.question: Rows in the shown confusion matrix are actual classes and columns are predicted classes. What are specificity and positive-class recall?
questions.code_snippet:
Predicted negative | Predicted positive
Actual negative: 90                 | 10
Actual positive: 20                 | 30
questions.explanation: Step 1: TN=90,FP=10,FN=20,TP=30 from the stated orientation. Step 2: Specificity=90/(90+10)=0.9. Step 3: Recall=30/(30+20)=0.6.

questions.question: For TP=30,FP=10,FN=20,TN=40, what is the positive-class F1 score?
A test set has 990 negatives and 10 positives. A model predicts every case negative. What are accuracy and positive-class recall?
questions.explanation: Step 1: TN=990,FN=10,TP=FP=0. Step 2: Accuracy=(990+0)/1000=0.99. Step 3: Recall=0/(0+10)=0, so high accuracy alone hides complete failure to retrieve positives.

questions.question: Two positive cases score 0.9 and 0.6; two negative cases score 0.8 and 0.1. Higher means more positive, and there are no ties. What is the empirical ROC-AUC?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Compare all 2*2=4 positive-negative pairs. Step 2: Score 0.9 beats both negatives; score 0.6 beats only 0.1. Step 3: Three winning pairs out of four give AUC=3/4.

questions.question: On a fixed binary dataset containing both classes, a classifier predicts positive whenever score>=threshold. As the threshold is lowered, which rates are guaranteed not to decrease?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Lowering the threshold can only add cases to the predicted-positive set. Step 2: TP and FP therefore cannot decrease. Step 3: Since actual-positive and actual-negative counts stay fixed, TPR and FPR cannot decrease; precision and accuracy can move either way.

questions.question: On a held-out dataset with a nonconstant response, SSE=150 and SST=100, where SST is measured about that evaluation set's response mean. Using R^2=1-SSE/SST, what is R^2?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Compute SSE/SST=150/100=1.5. Step 2: R^2=1-1.5=-0.5. Negative held-out R^2 is possible: these predictions have greater squared error than predicting the evaluation-set response mean.

questions.question: An OLS model has an intercept, n=21 observations, k=2 predictors excluding the intercept, and R^2=0.8. Using adjusted R^2=1-(1-R^2)(n-1)/(n-k-1), what is adjusted R^2?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Residual degrees of freedom are 21-2-1=18. Step 2: Adjusted R^2=1-(0.2)(20/18)=1-2/9=7/9. The predictor count excludes the intercept.

questions.question: An unconstrained OLS model with an intercept is refitted on exactly the same observations after adding a predictor. The response is nonconstant, and both residual degrees of freedom remain positive. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Training R^2 cannot decrease, but adjusted R^2 can decrease
options.B: A larger training R^2 guarantees a larger test-set R^2
options.C: Both training R^2 and adjusted R^2 must increase strictly
options.D: Training R^2 must decrease because there are more coefficients

questions.explanation: Step 1: The expanded model can reproduce the old fit by setting the new coefficient to zero, so minimized SSE cannot increase. Step 2: With the same SST, training R^2 cannot decrease. Step 3: Adjusted R^2 also penalizes lost degrees of freedom, so a small SSE improvement may not compensate.

questions.question: A pipeline chooses regularization strength using five-fold cross-validation and includes mean/standard-deviation feature scaling. Which procedure avoids validation-fold leakage?

options.A: Fit the scaler separately on each fold's training portion and apply it to that fold's held-out portion
options.B: Fit the scaler once on all observations before forming the folds
options.C: Choose the strength using the final untouched test labels first
options.D: Fit each fold's scaler using its held-out portion only and then train on all labels

questions.explanation: Step 1: Each validation fold must imitate unseen data. Step 2: Estimate scaling parameters from the corresponding training folds only. Step 3: Transform both portions with those parameters, fit the model on training data, and score the held-out fold.

questions.question: Across repeated representative iid train/validation splits, a highly flexible model has very low training error but much higher validation error. Which bias-variance diagnosis is most consistent with this pattern?

options.A: Proof that all validation labels are incorrect
options.B: High variance and overfitting; stronger regularization may improve generalization
options.C: High bias with equally poor training and validation fit
options.D: A guarantee that removing every penalty will improve validation performance

questions.explanation: Step 1: Low training error shows the model can closely fit its observed sample. Step 2: Repeatedly worse validation performance indicates poor generalization consistent with high variance. Step 3: Regularization can trade some extra bias for reduced variance, though improvement must be validated.

questions.question: In a two-coefficient constrained view of regularization, why can an L1 constraint promote exact zeros more readily than a squared L2 constraint?

options.A: The L1 feasible region has axis-aligned corners, while the L2 region has a smooth circular boundary
options.B: The L1 region is a smooth circle and the L2 region is a diamond
options.C: The L2 constraint requires every coefficient to be zero for any radius
options.D: The L1 constraint permits only positive coefficients

questions.explanation: Step 1: |beta1|+|beta2|<=t forms a diamond with corners on the coordinate axes. Step 2: beta1^2+beta2^2<=t forms a disk. Step 3: A loss contour can touch an L1 corner where one coefficient is zero; L2 shrinkage does not have those corners.

questions.question: For scalar beta, minimize (6-beta)^2+2*beta^2. No intercept is present. What is the ridge optimum?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Differentiate: 2(beta-6)+4beta=6beta-12. Step 2: Set the derivative to zero, giving beta=2. Step 3: The second derivative is 6>0, so this is the unique minimum.

questions.question: For scalar beta, minimize (1/2)(beta-3)^2+abs(beta). What is the lasso optimum?
questions.explanation: Step 1: On beta>0 the derivative is beta-3+1=beta-2, giving candidate beta=2. Step 2: The zero-point loss gradient -3 cannot be balanced by the penalty subgradient [-1,1]. Step 3: Convexity establishes beta=2 as the global minimum.

questions.question: Positive scores are [0.8,0.5] and negative scores are [0.5,0.2]. Empirical ROC-AUC gives half credit to a positive-negative tie. What is AUC?
questions.explanation: Step 1: There are four positive-negative pairs. Step 2: Positive 0.8 earns two wins. Positive 0.5 earns one win against 0.2 and half a win against 0.5. Step 3: AUC=(2+1+0.5)/4=3.5/4=7/8.

questions.question: Two nested OLS models use the same n=20 observations and an intercept. SST=190. The old model has k=2 predictors and SSE=90; the new has k=3 and SSE=86. Predictor counts exclude the intercept. Which change is correct?

options.A: Both R^2 and adjusted R^2 increase
options.B: R^2 increases; adjusted R^2 decreases from 8/17 to 37/80
options.C: R^2 decreases; adjusted R^2 increases from 8/17 to 37/80
options.D: Both R^2 and adjusted R^2 stay unchanged

questions.explanation: Step 1: SSE falls with fixed SST, so R^2 increases from 1-90/190 to 1-86/190. Step 2: SST/(n-1)=190/19=10. Step 3: Old adjusted R^2=1-(90/17)/10=8/17, about 0.4706. New adjusted R^2=1-(86/16)/10=37/80=0.4625, which is smaller.

questions.question: A no-intercept design satisfies X^T X=I and X^T y=[3,-0.5,2]. Compare lasso objective (1/2)||y-X beta||^2+sum_j abs(beta_j) and ridge objective (1/2)||y-X beta||^2+(1/2)sum_j beta_j^2. What are their coefficient vectors?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Orthonormality separates the loss into (1/2)sum_j(beta_j-z_j)^2 plus a constant, with z=X^T y. Step 2: Lasso soft-thresholds each z at 1: sign(z)max(|z|-1,0), giving [2,0,1]. Step 3: Ridge solves beta_j-z_j+beta_j=0, so beta=z/2=[1.5,-0.25,1].

questions.question: A no-intercept ridge problem minimizes ||y-X beta||^2+||beta||^2. Given X^T X=[[2,1],[1,2]] and X^T y=[3,0], what is its coefficient vector?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The normal equations are (X^T X+I)beta=X^T y, so [[3,1],[1,3]]beta=[3,0]. Step 2: The inverse is (1/8)[[3,-1],[-1,3]]. Step 3: Multiplying gives beta=[9/8,-3/8].

questions.question: Observe Y=theta+epsilon with theta=2, E[epsilon]=0, and Var(epsilon)=1. Estimate theta by beta_hat=Y/(1+lambda), the minimizer of (Y-beta)^2+lambda*beta^2. For lambda>=0, which lambda minimizes E[(beta_hat-theta)^2], and what is that minimum risk?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Bias is -2lambda/(1+lambda), and estimator variance is 1/(1+lambda)^2. Step 2: Estimation risk is (4lambda^2+1)/(1+lambda)^2. Step 3: Its derivative is (8lambda-2)/(1+lambda)^3, changing from negative to positive at lambda=1/4. Step 4: Substitution gives risk=0.8=4/5. This estimates theta, not a new noisy response.

questions.question: Two identical nonzero design columns equal x, with ||x||^2=1 and y=3x; there is no intercept. Compare ridge loss ||y-X beta||^2+beta1^2+beta2^2 with lasso loss ||y-X beta||^2+2(abs(beta1)+abs(beta2)). Which minimizers are correct?

options.B: Lasso uniquely gives (2,0); ridge uniquely gives (3,0)
options.C: Ridge uniquely gives (1,1); lasso permits every nonnegative pair with sum 2
options.D: Ridge permits every pair with sum 3; lasso has no minimizer

questions.explanation: Step 1: Write s=beta1+beta2; RSS=(3-s)^2. Step 2: For a fixed s, ridge minimizes beta1^2+beta2^2 at beta1=beta2=s/2. Its reduced loss is (3-s)^2+s^2/2, minimized at s=2, giving (1,1). Step 3: Lasso has penalty at least 2|s|, attained by any nonnegative pair when s>=0. Minimizing (3-s)^2+2|s| gives s=2, leaving all nonnegative decompositions optimal.

questions.question: Python 3 with pandas 2.3.x and NumPy 2.2.x. What centered list results after groupwise missing-value imputation and the all-missing-group fallback?

questions.question: Python 3 with pandas 2.3.x and NumPy 2.2.x. What two lists are printed after label-aligned assignment followed by positional assignment?

questions.explanation: Step 1: The Series assigned through loc aligns by labels, so a receives 100 and c receives 200 despite the requested row order c,a. Step 2: The first print in dataframe order a,b,c is [100,2,200]. Step 3: iloc then assigns list values by positions: c receives 7 and a receives 9, giving [9,2,7].

questions.question: A worker completes one job in 10 days at a constant rate. What fraction of the job is completed in one day?
questions.explanation: Daily work is total work divided by time: 1/10 of the job per day.

questions.question: A completes a job in 6 days and B in 3 days. Working together at constant additive rates, how many days do they need?
questions.explanation: Combined rate=1/6+1/3=1/2 job per day. Time=1/(1/2)=2 days.

questions.question: An inlet fills an empty tank in 8 hours; an outlet empties a full tank in 24 hours. With both open and constant rates, how many hours fill the empty tank?
questions.explanation: Net filling rate=1/8-1/24=1/12 tank per hour. Filling takes 12 hours.

questions.question: Twelve equally productive workers finish a job in 10 days. How many days would 15 such workers take at the same daily hours?
questions.explanation: The job needs 12*10=120 worker-days. Dividing by 15 gives 8 days.

questions.question: A vehicle covers 150 km in 3 hours at constant speed. What is its speed in km/h?
questions.explanation: Speed=distance/time=150/3=50 km/h.

questions.question: A car travels at 60 km/h for 5/2 hours. How many kilometres does it cover?
questions.explanation: Distance=speed*time=60*(5/2)=150 km.

questions.question: Convert 72 km/h to metres per second.
questions.explanation: Multiply km/h by 5/18: 72*(5/18)=20 m/s.

questions.question: A 120 m train passes a stationary pole at 54 km/h. How many seconds does the entire train take to pass?
questions.explanation: 54 km/h=15 m/s. Passing a pole requires travelling the train length, so time=120/15=8 seconds.

questions.question: A boat has still-water speed 10 km/h in a stream flowing at 2 km/h. What is its downstream speed in km/h?
questions.explanation: Downstream speed adds the current: 10+2=12 km/h.

questions.question: What is 18 percent of 250?
A quantity of 400 is increased by 15 percent. What is the new quantity?
questions.explanation: Increase=400*(15/100)=60. The new quantity is 400+60=460.

questions.question: Thirty out of 120 applicants qualify. What percentage qualifies?
questions.explanation: Qualification fraction=30/120=1/4. Multiplying by 100 gives 25%.

questions.question: An item costs 800 units and sells for 1000 units. What is the profit percentage on cost?
questions.explanation: Profit=1000-800=200. Profit percentage=(200/800)*100=25%.

questions.question: An item costs 500 units and sells for 450 units. What is the loss percentage on cost?
An item marked at 1000 units receives a 20 percent discount. What is its selling price in units?
An item costs 250 units. What selling price in units gives 20 percent profit on cost?
Two shares are in the ratio 3:5 and total 64 units. What is the smaller share?
questions.explanation: There are 3+5=8 ratio parts. Each part is 64/8=8, so the smaller share is 3*8=24.

questions.question: A:B=2:3 and B=18. What is A?
Five identical notebooks cost 150 units. At the same unit price, what do eight notebooks cost?
questions.explanation: Unit cost=150/5=30. Eight notebooks cost 8*30=240.

questions.question: A sum of 90 units is divided in the ratio 2:3. What is the first share?
questions.explanation: The first share is 2/(2+3) of the total: (2/5)*90=36.

questions.question: At 10 percent simple interest per year, what interest in units accrues on 1000 units over 2 years?
questions.explanation: Simple interest=P*r*t=1000*(10/100)*2=200.

questions.question: What is the total amount in units on 2000 units after 3 years at 5 percent simple interest per year?
What is the amount in units on 1000 units after 2 years at 10 percent annual compound interest, compounded yearly?
questions.explanation: Amount=1000*(1.10)^2=1210; the second year earns interest on the first year's interest too.

questions.question: On 1000 units at 10 percent per year for 2 years, how many units more is annual compound interest than simple interest?
questions.explanation: Compound interest=1210-1000=210. Simple interest=1000*0.10*2=200. Difference=10.

questions.question: A completes a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. At constant additive rates, how many days do they need together?
questions.explanation: Combined rate=1/12+1/18=5/36 job per day. Time=36/5 days, exactly.

questions.question: A and B together finish a job in 6 days. A alone takes 10 days. How many days does B alone take?
questions.explanation: B's rate=1/6-1/10=1/15 job per day, so B needs 15 days.

questions.question: A alone could finish a job in 15 days. A works for 5 days, then B alone finishes the remaining work in 10 days. How many days would B alone take for the whole job?
questions.explanation: A completes 5/15=1/3, leaving 2/3. B's daily rate is (2/3)/10=1/15, so the whole job takes B 15 days.

questions.question: Two inlets fill a tank in 6 hours and 8 hours respectively. An outlet empties it in 24 hours. Starting empty, how many hours fill it with all three open at constant rates?
questions.explanation: Net rate=1/6+1/8-1/24=(4+3-1)/24=1/4 tank per hour. Time=4 hours.

questions.question: An inlet alone fills a tank in 10 hours. A leak alone empties a full tank in 15 hours. Starting empty, how many hours fill the tank with inlet and leak both operating at constant rates?
